WILD •WEATHER. The south-west wind drives roughly through the trees, Bending the peevish poplar to the blast, stripping the beech, wkich, grasping to the last Her ragged rube, doth cuf.il before the breeze, - And wails and sighs as leaf by leaf she sees Her raiment scattered and her pride downcast. ,Then o'er the grim.hcrizon, gray and vast, Rise up a band of stalwart enemies: Great clouds climb up and seize the wind-beat sky; The pallid moon drifts in the rain-washed space, ' Where crape-like folds of enist drift round her form. 'Louder and louder now the wild winds cry, While patient Nature hides her weary face, And waits in faith the parsing of the storm.

The followingMetance of persistency on the part of a rejected admirer has perhape rarely been surpassed. The disappointed suitor followed the qoung woman and his more fortunate rival into the church—it was the churen of Burwash io Suseex—addresAng the bride-elect • from time to time in niteona tones, " Say 'no,' Martha; say 'no;' Martha"; and this he continued till the crucial question was put, "Wilt thou have this man to be thy wedded husband ?" As eooti es the fatal words. "I will,' had passed the bride's lips instead of the "No" which he had fondly hoped for, be turned away, and at once, and without any further remark, left the ehurch. CRILDRRN'fi ANsyreae.—Frem whatever cause it may 13,, there can be no doubt that the young people of Lon- don evince a sharpness not shown elsewhere. For example, who other than a London Board School boy could have given such A short account of the Conquest of Ireland" as " The Conquest of Ireland was begun in the year 1170, and is stilt ping on"? Nor is this talent confined to the bows, 53 a writer in a London newspaper demonstrated some lime ago. One girl, when asked how beef-tea was made, answered, "Buy a pot of beef extract. and billow the directions on the lid"; and a second gave "Cayenne pepper and Jamaica ginger" in reply to "What are warmth-producing foods?" But it was a boy. I think, who was asked what celerity was, and who, perhaps from experience, defined it as "some- thing to put hot plates down with." A pretty and sensible answer was returned to an. inspector the other day by a little girl, when asked to explain what was meant by "bearing false witness against your neigh- bour." "It was," she said, "when nobody did nothing, and somebody went and told of it" Another gentle- man of the same class was examining some country lads, and asked one of them if he knew what vowels ' were. "Fowls, sir ?" answered the boy, "why, fowls be chickens!" Equally naive was a little boy whose uncle inquired of him how he liked going to school. "I like going well enough." was his ingenuous reply. "but I don't like staying when I get there." Still more amus- ing was the retort made by a small boy to an old gentle- Wan who, on his twelfth birthday, hoped that he would 'improve in wisdom, knowledge, and virtue." - getting, by degrees, to Henry and his bad habits. some- how or other, the nervous tissue of the cerebrum 'VOWS to "the thoughts that are allowed free course in the mind. How, Peience hardly ventures to guess as yet: but for the sake of illustratlort, kit us imavine that certain thoughts of the mind run to and fro, in the ner- vous substance of the cerebrum until they hay;:t made a 'Etty, a rut, there: busy traffic in the same Wei 2f thoughts will always be kept up. for there is the eaSVI way for them to run in. -Now, take the child with as inherited tendency to a resentful temper: he has begun to think resentful thoughts; finds them easy and grati- fying; he goes on; evermore the rut deepens, and the ugly traffic becomes more easy and natural, and resent- fulness is rapidly becoming himself, that trait in his char- acter which people couple with his name. But, one custom overcometh another. The watchful mother sets up new tracks in ether directions; and she sees to it, that while she k leading new thoughts through the new rut, the old, deeply worn "way of thinking" is quite dis- used. sow, the cerebrum is in a state of rapid waste land rapid growth. The new growth takes shape from the new thoughts; the old rut is lost in the steady /waste; and the child is reforme,ct, physically, as wt.ll as. morally and mentally. That th,s' Belleirt t;;;u6 or the Vrebrum.should be -finis the instrument of the mind need not stl?prise US WI% we think how the muscles and joints of the ttui., the vocal organs of the singer, the r,ST4 finger-ends Ot the watchmaker, the palate of the tea- taster, grew to the uses they are steadily put to; and, much more, bct'i in the case of brain and of bodily organs, grow to the uses they are earliest put to. This meets in a wonderful way the case of the parent who eels himself to cure a moral failing. He sets up the course of new thoughts, and hinders those of the past, until the new thoughts shall have become automatic and run of their own accord. All the time a sort of disinte- gration is going on in the place that held the disused ! thoughts; and here is the parent's advantage. If the boy return (as, from inherited tendency, he still may do), to his old habits of thought, behold there is no more place for them in his physical being; to make a new place is a work of time, and in this work the parent can -overtake and hinder him without much effort. Here, indeed, more than anywhere, "Except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it;" but, surely, intelligent co-operation in this divine work Is our bounden duty and service.—Murrap'i Magazine.

• ,SOrICO. We have Ude- surfeit of Municipal matters lately: They are, after. 14/4stenewhat dull, and inclined to be pr', eo"we.will take a • iest- from them, and try something -else. ;Let,. us launch into the wonid of song. • "Mirsic bath obarms," sings the poet, and it is charming indeed to listen to the familiar ballads I that we all lover so well, if they are well sung, whatever may be the effect on the" savage breast" over which music. is appposed to have a soothing influence. But, .putting aside, say, some of the elaborate singing a the...pFera stage, rather berogd the vocal powers of,. thaerdinary run of man, and the fashionable songs that fashionable artistes lave to trill in the language-ot Italy or France—such, an fact, as Ko-go-aings—,-avbat can you really call the popular songs of the deys? Put the aristocracy on one side altogether for the nonce—for there is an aristocracy &adz-democracy in song as in anything else—and ask yourself thequestion as it will pre- I sent itself to those of the anasses. The educated person, with a culiffrited.manical taste, might soon' answer it to isle or her entire satisfaction, but what a vast number there are on this eattlicotours,,and! On this little speck .called Eogla.ad, who are noe: educated, and whose tastes ,arelfree fro& cuttiva-, tion, in the ordinary acceptance tir the word. Still, there is an ianate•love of music in most people—in' the English people in ,partiaiklar—and the man whose humble duty itoia to labourarith the hod may share it with a peer attlie realm. One person likes one.dass of songs; another likes another class, and so on, and the .moro you think of this diversity of opinion the harclt it is to say what really are the popular songs. ;tilt is, after all, purely a matter of opinion, and a guestion that can be answered in many different waya,nccording to the fancy of individuals. There are -.some -songa, of course—songs of love and of war, afaadventures by land and by sea, of sentiment and of humour—that enjoy. and always will do, an .aluaosa universal popularity. There are songs-that stir the emotions, bring tears to the eye, and songs that -arinke your face broaden with smiles, and. your heart feel merry. You can hear them anywhere and .everywhere. At the Sunday school conies*, or in the parlour of the Pig and Whistle; in thedmaring- rooms of the rich, and in the cottages-of the poor. la far-off lands as well as at home, at seaas wall as ea land, in the barrack-room and on the deck of the troopship, they are sung, and sung again. d have hesx4 them sung in the village" Pub" to the serv- ing otia fiddle, and I have heardthem to the twang- ing of a banjo under the Southern Cross. r.3.-can know the kind of songs I mean—who has not heard them? And who does notaitill wish to hear them/ But there is another class, and a widely popular class, too. They are not often heard in the drawing room; they are not, as a matter of fact, very select, but still they are popular among a numerous class. Launched in the first instance from the stage of some music hall, they go the rounds of the public house" free and easy," and the circle of their acquaintance becomes wider and wider. Though not "select," it must not be taken for granted that • they are all of an objectionable nature. Some, both as regards words and rhythm are very good in their way, but certainly others am uncompromisingly vulgar. Some, that have an obvious double mean- ing, are the worst. It is far from Ko-Ko's intention to disparage all songs that are sung in the public+ house. It is no uncommon thing to hear a really good sang in the snug bar parlour, or more commo- dious singing root, of a local house of call; a seuti- mental verse or two, or a comic ditty; and, as a rule, bar the lower class of singing rooms, it is the exception rather than the rule to hear anything objectionable. But it must be confessed that there are places where songs and character sketches are given that would bring the blush to the cheek of any right-thinking man. The evil tendency of such songs cannot be doubted, but I would fain believe that they are not included among the popular ones. You may ask—what is all this alsout ? Simply the outcome of a little reflection after reading one of those flimsy looking song sheets, purchasable at a penny each, 'that ars so clear to the hearts of errand lads, and hundreds of our juvenile popula- tion of the working sort—and to hundreds of their elders, too. Perhaps, however, there are many others who never had the curiosity, or the inclina- tion to look at these production.. They are worth while passing under review, for they have a wider clieatele than might be supposed. Each sheet con- tains a selection of songs both numerous and mis- cellaneous specially the latter. Some are pass- ably good, others laughable, and some ridiculously silly. Let us look at one of these sheets, vilely naof tell on vile paper. It begins pretty well with a couple 7f. pathetic verses, in which the singer bids t adieu to the hinible cot " where first he saw the light of day" prefflus to speeding his way to a foreign clime. Then, to the favourite air ef " The Anchor's weighed" comes a lively song under the title of "The Pawnshop's near." Well have one verse and—don't forget the tune "The gin had risen to her eve, When last we lingered at the door ; I plainly saw she'd shortly try, To pledge her shawl to get some more. " Dear Ted ! she cried,' Oh, let me haste away, I want more gin, I really cannot stay; mag, ! poorly without it shall be, The TZrnstioii 12nr—o:ekl-bye, remember roe," Again, to the tune of "Gaily the Troubebr." three four-line verses Chant the affetiort -ei the " Bluebottle," that Much abused awl representative of justice, for the desire.bls cook. The end line of each verse runs—" Cookey, dear cookey, dear, come to thy Sam," and it is easy to imagine this, and the i preceding song, " going down well in some corn- panies. 'Squint-eyed Molly Gee "is the wail of a disappointed one who has wasted his affections and spare cash on the cross-eyed. fair one, who, however, he does not want to see again, as she has gone off with " s'mother fool." Turning over the leaf,l happen across another rub at the blue-coated one, to be trolled out to the air of " Mother kiss me in your dreams." Here is the last verse.—

Oft again I hope to see That fat cookey at her door, Handing forth tit-bits to me, As she oft has done bofore. % I, as from her street I stroll, Wheve around all dreary seems, Think as my inside dotli roll, Cookey gave me ham and beans." The next selection, "Skip the gutter," belongs to the" spoke 'class, where you sing averse and then interpolate a sentence or two of prose. Thus, after the first verse—" Yes, my friends, you must always imagine you have got the best of everything, and why? Because imagination is a wonderful satis- fler,for instance if,when you sea a pretty little girl and you imagine you have already kissed her, although perhaps you may not ' have been any nearer to her than to smack your own lips, still you will feel half satisfied, but then if you wish to kiss the little girl properly you must walk boldly up to her, look straight into her pretty little face, smile at her and say— Skip the gutter, tra, la, la ! Tottie do you love me P Ting, ting, au revoir " girls there's none above me, If you like me tell me so, do not let me linger ? Tottie if you love me, oh! /squeeze my little finger." Again—" Clean your boots, sir, clean your boots, is now the London cry; Veil clean your boots upon your foots, be veather vet or dry. A stunning go for seedy beau, and peg-top nobby swells, As Day and Martin meets the nose, while each street corner

tells,"—(Chorus)—" That for a penny yon mitsy shine' and cut a first class figure to valk with Julia—divine—(spoken: OILI liow. blackened up like any nigger r "Yea—l'm the boy to annihilate your bunions, and make your ' coriferid-hot—buriCeibliff-vitlrMetion that's a capital cure, ain't it? and saves you a guinea vttli • the eluo-ipopo-dist, Now, I don't 'fish to be:peterl —but if there's any Of you young swells he o- night wots got bad corns on your feet, come to aise. —only a penny-Land ra- Clean your boots, sir, clean your boots, is nowtbe London cry • , „ Istanding Yell clean your boots upon Your foots, I'm ready On the other side of tbeTeheet "The Bald-headed Swell " grows eloquent over the attractions :of-ibis "mash," who, by the way, "has vanished like a' cloud of mist." She appears to be a remarkable young person. Besides having ." a corporation like an air balloon," and "a paralytic pimple on her tongue"—" She's a pimple with some whiskers on her cheek, The hair upon her head, is a -fiery Shade of red, To match-the lovely blossom on her beak" —and, all j,in in please— "Has anyone seen her, the flower of Pali Mall, Matilda come back to your bald-headed swell, If anyone's seen her will they kindly tell, We will meet in the Sweet Bye and Whether Matilda ever did came back is shrouded in uncertainty, but one would think be-of the bald head would have preferred net to be 'on speaking terms. But perhaps he thought the balthhead set off? " Topsy from de Georgia State" warbles— Hey said de fun would soon begin, (Symphony) „ So I skipped the gutter an' Baird right in, '(Symphony' An' now I's here, I oh I I'se bound to let yeu know, 11 I'se a jet black gal from PlunkoVal„ - -•- t My sweetheart's Julius Crow, An' when he's hitch'd to me, You bet we'll have a spree, And if you get a chance to come to tie dance, You mustn't tickle me." It is wonderful how a stegro-minstvel,ditty, ssuig to a lively tune, "takes,' with a good ." vamping' accompaniment. Thus the adventures of "A ship load of niggers looking happy and well, ,Gwine to ole Virginny in de mont"'— ' ' Gwine to 'ole Virginnv in de morn, honey, T'o the land of de possum and de coon, Where de chickens roost low, e.nd de water melonegrow. We'll be infloo-en-shul pussons peoty soon:" After investigating, a little further, me come across a person who must be a blood relation of the damsel that was the object of the search of our friend the Held Headed SwelL She appears under' the name of "Scarlet Fever Jane," hails from iJersey, and "She's as pretty as the bird they call a 'hear I" She, in fact, somew hat takes tbe :palm tirom the other one, for the song sets forth that she tiles an "ironfoundry cheek,' and, in addition, "iiihe lives on Cheshire cheese, And her face would lake you sneeze, And right down 'her back she wears a chinesn tail; Her teeth they shine likelead, sh:o's a bald spot on her head, Her ears would -hold a boatel full of rain; Her mouth looka like a tunnel, anditer nose looks like a funnel ; tatgeot, guess-what-is-it Jane "- 1a Jane, my Jane, my pretty Jane, Comes to the workhouse once again, Tourare tongue-tied in your thumbs, .awd have Cerli3 upon your gums, You'ie my flip flap, somersault, acrobatic Jane.' But perhaps I am picking out all the silliest items on the Awe. Be it so. Though silly, though nauseatiw, they are popular. It can't be denieW, that some pf the songs, especially when sung amid fumes of stobacco and clatter of glasses, must have I a desneraiidu" ig tendency, especially so in the case of the young-rand the young go to public houses and mune halls--nowadays -far more often than some of you fond rps.rents think. I must not, however, condemn the whole sheet, for it also contains songs that are appreciated the world over—standard pieces that .av,o too well-known to need reproduce tion. There are other songs, too, political satires among the number, whiebtif not elevating, are enough to amuse and entertain. One of the political character sings the praises 4f the heroes of Waterloo and Trafalgar, and draws a Very untlivourable comparison between the days ,of those exploits and the present. For— .

"We have reniews in our days, We shun the rain in our days. For these are our umbrella days With a gingham down at Aldershot. We can't be brave in our days, We don't show valour now-a-days, These "peace at any price" days, With the Lib'rals in full swing." Just another quotation, and then I will leave the reader to grapple with the question of what are, after all, the "songs of the day." It is a second ;Awe of "Young Hearts."— Golden is a woman's smile When the heart is young. Hazel eyes are without guile When the heart is young. Lips of lovers when they meet, Kisses low and kisses sweet, Laugh away all cold deceit, When the heart is young."

Gret trees, whe,er t' childer played i' swarms, Below ther welcome shade, 0 swing they long, bare, lanky arms, Bi th' wild winds to/A an' swayed. Deawn th' loyne—wheer th' honeysuckles grew, An' blossomed, heigh o'er th' rest; O'er th' ruddy rooase, an' bells so blue ;- o's lonely neaw. Iv yo'll peep thro' _.Yo'll see a empty nest. An' th' hedge fair sobs as t' wind sweeps on, An' carries th' deod lecives past; Id sobs an' sighs for th' calm days gone— Wild lVinter's comin' fast, Yon hillside slopes rooase slantin' up• , To t' gowden Summer sky; .o gowd an' green wP buttercups An' grass times gone by; Then; !its o' places, whitened o'er, Showed daisies clustered theer ; Neaw, th' een kornd find thad flowery floor, Th' breawn hillside's blank as t' dreary moor Witheawt a charm to cheer; An' dull mist slowly winds abeawt Id top, an' stops at last, Till rain drops deawn, an' tempests sheawt,— For Winter's comb' fast. Th' owd farm heawse, wi' t' low pooarch i' front, Looked nice an' cosy, when Th' breet sun shooen warm an' cheery on 't, An' t' throstle sung i' th' glen. While th' rindlin' brook, so cool an' clear, Murmured a gentler song •, An' posies layned o'er V banks to hear Id music, babbled sweetly theer. O's changed, for fierce an' strong, Th' rain drives neon id, thatch an' wo' ; An' th' brooks fair fit to brast Id banks, id storms an' tumbles so, 'Cause Winters' comin' fast. An' nearer hooam, P th' smooky teawn, Wheer Labour's built id hives; Wheer theawstnds toil while t' gaffers freawn, Youths, husbands, maids, an' wives, 0 strive an' tew for brass, an' thrutch Poor wayklin's back to t' wo'. Ther's hundreds, fast i' Misery's clutch, As tramp, for wark thre rain an' slutch, Au' leet o' twat at o id's hod a cheerless sect to see Poor warkers trampin' t' nast, WP nowt to do, Trade slack an' dreei An' Winter clmin' fast, O t' chilly winds fro' th' lkst, an' North, VW sleet, an' hail, an' rain, Are Winter's heralds, t'ellin' th' Earth's" Vast millions, strevt an' plain, I' langwidge—Natui's ruffest sooart— As t' time o' sunshine's flown. An' th' beggar lad, or king at th' coourt, Mun, for a while, be Winter's spooart, Till Spring's soft trumpets blown. Plain fooak are fain' to hutch bi th' fire At neat, when baggin's To jooak on tawir—booath child an' sire, O'er t' Winter comin' fast.

MR. T. W. Lain IN PARLIAMENT.

On Saturday, in the House of Commons, in the course of a debate on the detention of the British troops at Suakim, Mr. ,T . W. Legh, M.P., for the Newton Division, said that when Mr. Morley and gentlemen on the opposite side attacked.the Govern.; ment on the question of Suakim, it must be ration- - ally admitted that they had a strong case, and the history of our dealings there was not such as to give us any pride. He was personally inclined to regard it ass little short of a national disgrace (heir, hear). He appealed to the Government to carefully consider the suggestion made by the hon. member for Kirkcaldy, that Suakimishauld be handed over to the Italians. In 1885, when Mr. Gladstone was in office, a state of things existed in Massowah similar to .that now existing in Suakim, and the Italian Government were thenrequested by the right hon. gentleman—who showed remarkable generosity (slaughter), for it wao perfectly obvious that he had no right to do anything of tho kind—to take pos- session of Massowah. The. Government had now an ample opportunity for exhibiting a similar generosity. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He presumed that,from the necessities of his position' the Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs wasreluctantto state what he (Mr. Legh) believed to be one of the „real reasons for despatching British troops—viz., the fear ;that Suakim would fall into the hands of an unfriendly Power, and that, in fact, the French Government would takeva fancy for the place (hear, hear.) Therefore, in. sending British troops to Suakim, her Majesty's Government were guarding it , against such a contingency, as well as against the Dervishes and Arab tribeswho were threatening it. The Italians were convinced of the advantages of Ma.ssowali,
‘I /III" I°l 'l4'a

and there should not be much difficulty ,—,,oaaing them to go to Suakim. By so doing we would please everybody (Mr. Labouchere : "Except the French," and laughter.) It was bad enough already to have a French agent at Cario, but, for goodness' sake, don't let them have an opportunity for meddling in the Soudan (hear, hear.) They should please the Italians, and it .could not possibly signify to the Arabs and Dervishes 'whether they fought with, the Italians or with the English (laughter), and it would,bethp ;neans of keeping ourselves free from the disagreeable consequences which must inevitably follow the despatch of the British troops, to Suakiin. .
WARRINOTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse on Friday morning. The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided, and there were also present Messrs. W. Log, Darbyshire, Jolley, °Went, Pen- nington, W. Houghton. J. Houghton,.Swinton,.J. Rylands, Grange; S. Sutton (clerk), -Dr. Sephton (medical officer), W. Owen - (surveyor), and F. Kerfoot (inspector). THE HOSPITAL QUESTION.—The question of providing an infectious diseases hospital for the Authority's district was brought forward by the Clerk, but Mr. W. Houghton suggested that it would be better to leave the matter over till the establishment of County Councils, and he moved that they defer further consideration for six months. This was agreed to. NAVVIES HOTS FOE RIXTOM.--The Clerk said that he had as instructed written to the Ship Canal contractor relative to the overcrowding that was taking place at Rixton, and asking if it was intended to provide more navvies huts at that place. He had received a letter in reply stating that it was proposed tO put up some more huts at Itimton.—Lethe course of some conversation it was stated that as the_ number of men employed on the canal was being reduced for the -Winter it wouldino- bably lead to an abatement of overcrowding. u itiAL ACCOMMODATION AT RIXTON.—A parochial committee was appointed for Rixton-with-Glazebrook to take into consideration the providing of increased burial accomodation for the townihip. MORE LAMPS WANTED.—Mr.Tennington suggested the desirability of providing lamps for streets outside the borough boundary and moved that the Warrington Car- portion be written to in order to ascertain the price per lamp they would charge for the main road.2-Mr. Darby- ' shire-roved as an amendment that Lo' action be taken ' until they saw what steps -would be taken as to extending the borough boundary.—The motion was,how- ever, agreed to by six votes to four. THE MAKING or STREBTS.—The Medical Officer in his report referred to the wet and dirty state of streets off Liverpool-road, awl Mr. J. Rylands moved that Messrs. Pennington, Jolley, Greening and Heaton, be appointed a committee to take into consideration the question of making these streets.—Mr. Pennington seconded this proposal which was agreed to.
A lIAIR-DRESSER'S DIFFICULTIES.

I believe, as yet unknown to its paten- tees, in that alrealy well-known and highly valued liniment St. Jacobs Oil. A few days ago, the tonsorial one was hobbling about in an agony of mind and body, brought on by premonitory twinges in his foot, which experience warned him fore- shadowed a touch of gout. Prompted more by curiosity than by any great faith in the efficacy of the treatment, he applied a dressing of. St. Jacobs Oil to the suffering member, and the next morning, to the surprise of the household and his own delight, all traces of the complaint had vanished. This reads very much like a puff for a patent medicine, lAA it is nothing of the sort. I know nothing of the St. Jacobs Oil people ; we have never been favoured with an advertise- ment from them, and probably never shall be, but the above fact is simply narrated from motives of eornmon humanity. Mrs. G. Angold, 7, Maude-road, London, was allicted with chronic rheumatism for four years. She found n• relief from medicines, and was Induced to ,nse St. Jacobs Oil. One application reduced the swelling of the ankles and knees, and two more ap;plications removed all pain. Mr. J. Wilkinson, 88, Bentham-road, South Hackney, London, suffered from rheumatism in his feet _and. legs

for twenty years. One bottle of St. Jacobs Oil drove away all pall], and brought about an effectual cure. Mr. Henry Ricketts, Trym Cottages, Westbury, Gloucestershire, was a great sufferer from rheumatism icor o*r two years. Then he used St. Jacobs Oil. One application entirely relieved him of pain ; this health is now fully restored, and the disease has never returned._ _ _ _

The Christian Globe says: "A man employed at Central Fish Market, London, was for three years help- less with rheumatism, and after having been sent to three different hospitals was declared incurable. After three days use of St. jacobs Oil, he could use his arm without pain. Continuing the uee of it, all pain' swell- ing, and stiffness, disappeared. He is now cured, and at work." . _

St. Jacobe Oil Acts like magic. Its curative powers are simply marvellous. It conquers pain quickly and surely. It goes right to the spot. It cures when every- thing else has failed. A single trial will convince the most incredulous. has cured thousands of cases of rheumatism and neuralgia which have resisted treat- ment for the greater part of a lifetime.

The Council of the National Rifle Association on Wed- nesday held a meeting to formally determine the site of the annual rifle shooting competition. Staines was generally voted too small, and Cannock Chase too far from London. Ultimately Brookwood was adopted, under certain conditions. KAY'S COMPOUND Essence of Linseed, Aniseed, Senega, Squill, Tel% Ito., with Chlorodyne, 90., 13}(1., Ace. Advt. TER PARNELL INQUIRY —The Parnell Commission resumed its sittings on Tuesday. Some evidence as to intimidation by moonlighting in county Cork in 1881 was taken. Canon Griffin said he went to Millstreet in 1872. The district was then very peaceable. In 1881-82 it became disturbed. Cross-examined, he said that thous- ands of good priests approved of the League. Witness believed that it fostered malice. On Wednesday, at the opening, Sir Chas. Russell suggested that the wearisome- ness of the inquiry would justify their lordships in not sitting beyond the end of next week, and then adjourning. Sir Henry James concurred, and the President acceded. Further evidence was then taken as to the condition of Millstreet. Head Constable Hobblns said ho attended a meeting at Millstreet on the 15th August, 1886, when Dr. Tanner said the people took the field and died in 18137, and might be forced to do the same in 1887. Richard Williams, Fermoy, deposed that he was threatened and shot in the groin for taking a farm formerly occupied by Thomas Ihmell. Sergeant O'Brien deposed that Williams was boycotted. Cornelius .Regen., farmer, BrOadford, Cklarleville. said that in March, 1888, his house was fired Into because of his having paid rent. The League condemned the outrage. James Walsh, secretary of the Kiltimagh branch of the League, explained the working of the plan of cam- paign. Sir Charles Russell objected to the plan of cam- .paign being included in the inquiry, but the President , moved that it was admissible. In cross-examination by Sir C. Russell,. the witness admitted pilfering the funds of the League and other dishonourable 'actions. On Thursday Patrick Molloy who had refused to attend on a subpcena, was brought up from Dublin on a war- rant, and it having been agreed that his evidence should be taken next day, he wag removed. in , custody. The chief witness of the day was a man named Michael Burke, who gave evidence concerning the circumStances of the murder of Lord MountmorreS. The cress- lexamination of the witness is to be resumed at a later stage. On Thursday arrangements were completed for proof on the 20th inst. on the question of arrestments in Mr. Parnell's Scotch action against, the "Times."

HER BROTHER'S KEEPER.
• - BY MRs. J.—K.- SPENDER, -Author _of "Mr. " Parted Lives," "Both in the Wrong," " Ile-collections of a CountrY'Doetor,* "Trust Me," &e.

• CHAPTER Xtir.• A FRAY WITH TIIE POACHERS. "I should ntt regret it if I were you. He had always fine theories in his dreams, but responsibility would have been a sort of .nightmare to him. I can understand that in his better moods he would

do anything to avoid the burden of it. lie is one of those people who ought to have lived in the days when men went into monasteries to avoid the struggle of life. And so long as these new friends do . not jar on his artistic susceptibilities, and he thinks they can help him to fight his spiritual enemies, so long—if I were yon—l would not interfere," wrote Fielding .to Ursula, in his attempt to make the best
of whaF had happeUed. And considering that Ilityniond was nearly of age —having deferred his going to Oxford till he was twenty—no interference would have done any good.

'Ursula, who was, always ansiona .wherever her brother was concerned; had already thought, with a sort of terror, of the necessity of going back to Abbeyford. The consciousness of, being under a aloud, and 'the certainty that some of his old friends might cut him or be Only likely to speak to him for the sake of his sister, would have made a further residence at S Agatha intolerable to Raymond's vanity. Thinlafig of this, she agreed with Fielding that the step her brother had taken was not altogether to be regretted. For Raymond had a constant craving for popu- larity which always asserted itself, and the tacit avoidance of tho Abbeyford people, even if that avoidance had not taken the form of open incivility, would have been horrible for one of his .disposition to bear. Generally speaking a man can struggle against tka condemnation of• popular opinion' and bear to be made a public example of, though a woman cannot. But even Fielding's friendship had failed to give Raymond courage of this sort. In his unhappy predicament he had turned against Fielding. If Ursula had once hoped to supply her brother with an example which Might ennoble him—an exansple to be imitated, and which might -ima.k. Raymond wish to be such a -man as Fielding—that lope had failed her now. She determined never to try such an experiment again, and her heart failed hers little when Fielding acknowledged that he did not think the present im- pulsive choice would be one likely to last. " It will last him for a time," he said," till the old. craving returns, and till he again thinks it his duty to secure for himself as many as possible of the pleasures of life. I would try and persuade Dr. Havard .to leave him alone for the ,present. Much may be done if they can make ateetotaler of. him—if you like when the term is over I will go to Abbeyford and speak to the doctor about it." That will be good and kind of you" said the girl. She herself went back to S.- Agatha's and did her best to construct some sort of new, existence out of the ruins of the past. • But her plan. i for Raymond had been so, much to her —he had occupied so much the position of the baby in a maternal life—that it was difficult for her first eager aspirations, which had Centered in her brother, to be succeeded by others as yet. There were times when certain memories could not

be suppressed. She ghiated over these exciting memo- ries, even when they were most painful, as women are apt to do; turning the knife in their wounds. ,In the summer it was bad enough, when the fragrance of the new morn hay, the last songs of the lingering birds, the butterflies flitting across the lawn,' di the long sweeps of billowy foliage melting in thScdistance towards the village of Langhorne, re- called tfilmghts of faithful Peggy, and her pretty in- valid mot*r. But the autumn was most depressing to her. Perhaps because there is no season like the autumn for seeing a country, and the very beauty of everything reminded her of the days when she and Ray—who had been till lately so übiquitous in her life—had taken such genuine long walks together after the heat of summer was over; or perhaps be, cause of a sea of awful silence, oppressive to her cheerful nature,which came with damp and obscuring mists on certain of the dullest days. She welcomed everything that would break the spell of this silence, even if it were a gale of wind tearing amongst the trees, and strewing the paths with broken branches. She hailed the depredator with delight; he had something more to say to her than the constant and somewhat wearisome patter of good Mrs. Wilson's stream of commonplaces. Anything to break the tense atillness.i of her life.

She forgot that she had once thought it cruel -to slaughter the pheasants, and liked to hear the whirr of a covey, or to see a rabbit scudding across her path almost as well as Hubert Allston, who— . letting bygones be bygones—with sonic faint hopes for the future would occasionally meet her in her lonely rambles and walk by her side, throwing away his cigar and "cocking his ears," as Ursula said, to listen to the sounds which stirred his pulses and put him on the alert. His instinct, as the drctor said, was that inherited propensity for sport which comes to Englishmen as a natural endowment in this colder climate where the stock of caloric needs to be replenished. Ray, in the old days, had also watched the -rabbits scudding away to their bur- rows amongst the roots of the tall hr trees, but if he had tried to shoot, anything he had generally missed. Ursula, 'as Sir Thomas admitted, was-considerably toned down. She was becoming much snore like an ordinary sensible young woman—the product of Eng- lish climatic influences, English education, English environmeiit. She had gained a new modesty about her own opinions, and was no longer always quoting learned books and getting out of her depth. She even seemed to be aware of the impressiveness of the baronet's personality. The supreme dignity of his presence had not hitherto been admitted by this re- calcitrant young woman. But now—was it because she was in low spirits she had even ceased to inquire with any warmth of interest into the rights of the numerous people she employed, bringing to ear upon them such light, as she had been able to imbibe from a hasty study of Toynbee and Mill. "Rights I" as Sir Thomas told her, was an ob- jectionable word, for men as well as for women—it came in with atheism and the French Revolution. , She tried to debate the point, but the conversation dagged,and the topic died out gradually without ob- jectionable exeiteMent. ".Perhaps it is wise for me to give it up. I shall never do anything with them," she said to Margaret Havard, to that lady's intense delight. Margaret even waxed sentimental and told her friends that the motherless girl during her life in Paris had been like a diamond encrusted- in earth, or set 'in by inferior stones. Margaret on occasions got confused in her metaphors, but when she en- larged on it to Hubert Allston, that inconsistent young fellow was strangely silent. He was not quite sure in his secret heart that he had not pre- ferred Ursula in the rough diamond stage. It was the old Ursula just as she was, with all her defects, whom he had loved so desperately. He felt like the man whose young wife had in his absence pur- chased some cosmetic for improving her complexion, and who rant. meet him tnumphantly without her freckles. That husband missed the freckles, as Hubert missed Ursula's eccentricities. She could not tell him that though her body was walking by him, her spirit Was absent with Raymond. Poor Ray- mond was to others a contemptible failure—they thought themselves well rid of him ; but all such opinions affected her not. As she gazed at the soft •greys and delicate blues of the horizon, she did not hear what her companion said. She was think- inn. of the old cottage at Langhorne. Every turn. of'the road recalled Ray in his childhood, when the number of the field paths which they two could follow had been almost infinite, and when they had first wandered to S. Agatha's and watched the fences green with mess, or the grim outposts of the gates with alarming "trespass boards," which shut them outfrom the woods and plantations of the more stately and richly-timbered park. Those woods were all Ursula's now—looking so bright in their autumnal tints, with trees so small and smooth in the dis- tance that y6u wished to stroke their velvety tops as they .Stretched downwards towards the river in the dip of the hill. Years ago there had been deer in the park. Ursula had so far come round to Sir Thomas's opinions as to wish to preserve them again. The lakelet had been drained till it was glassy, and re- flected the shadows of the willows and the silver birches under which the fisher might dangle his rod if fish could be properly preservel Two hindrances were in the way—,one was the necessity for lowering rents, which even the old baronet was fain to admit to be necessary, and which, with the sudden drain caused by the repayment of all Raymond's debts, had left her short of money for some months ; the other \was "those rascals of poachers," as Sir Thomas always called them. Indeed, behind Ursula's back lie was still wont to

div.p: lament that his office had been discredited, and that' an attempt had been made to wrest his authority from , him; adding that since a "bit of a girl' had put her finger in the pie, and infected his own on with her "cursed radicalism," the poachere , had been more -daring than ever. "There ought to • he no such thing as a woman landowner," growled , Sir Thomas. Beautiful stnisets Isere common in autninuf aear Abbeyford, and on the evening when Wilfrid Fielding ' paid his promised visit to Dr. Bayard great masses of shadow veiled the zenith, but at the east there was a band of ted and purple which, ,grow- . ing larger as he Rued at it, seemed to 'throw out mosques and. minarets confused with the architec- ture of the fine old city, floating at last in a sea of sold, till the red disc of the sun sank behind the hills . ui a general conflagration. , . That evening there was a desperate affray between the four keepers at Allston Park and a gang of *bout "six poachers. The men were poaching rabbits and game with nets. -The keepers ' were trying - to arrest them, when the poachers, who were armed with pitchforks and bludgeons, turned upon one of the keepers, and stabbed him with a pitch- i fork, • inflicting serious wounds, and knocking' -! another severely about the head. A man with a red - beard, chestnut hair,, and dark blue eyes was said , to be foremost in the fray urging the other men ; on. It was the same fellow—so said the goesip-- ' who had appeared on a former -occasion, turning the heads of the boozers in the public-house , when Miss Campion's game had been taken. He and the other%men made good their retreat, but one of their, number was taken prisoner and brought before the justices. , This event made a considerable impression on Ursula, who, as Sir Thomas said, had been often on the edge of doing some other wild and im- practical things, hatl.,not he or Dr. Havarti con- stantly remonstrated. Sir Thomas was, indeed, in a white heat of anger, rabid with rage, talking more than usual about "we men," and supplementing his en" comiums on his own, sex by uncomplimentary allu- . Ehons to "those fools of women." He declared that he felt sure Miss Campion must suspect the names of at' least some of the escaped delinquents, to which sh(r answered with a touch of her old perversity that. if she did "wild horses should not drag the informa- tion out of her," at least so long as Sir Thomas wee one of the magistrates. 1 , The quarrel ran high, and was not bettered by the. fact that Hubert conceiveda jealous aversion to Field-, jug and attached a, false importance to his visit to Dr. - Havard. Fielding, who had been counted one of the safest firsts of his year, had come out second in his final examination, and Ursula knew that the disappointment was probably owing to hie devoted attendance on her brother. Ile made light of the matter ; but she reproached her- self without reason e . It seemd to • her as if she were fated' never to do. a kindly thing, or take an, active part in any movement for the good of °there,) but it led to something perplexing and annoying. She had long ceased to try to better the poor people of S. Agatha's, being content with offering. monet to Mr. Bond, who still continued to conduct the; services in the little chapel in her grounds.. Be • there was now an instinctive revolt in her againee the suffering in the world, which made her tun*. with averted eyes feom the abyssei of dogradat7on which some of her fellow-creatures were struggling. Wickedness was not only not beautiful, but .hi' poverty which led to contemptible shifts was revolt-, mg to her also. She could not trust herself to 'fac more diss,greeables just at present. , There was in her, as there was in Rayniond, a con' 'Mina' craving after happiness. At this time she had the habit of putting all her perplexities before her in a sort of drilled rank and file, the lesser ones ranging to greater ones, that she might meet the gnawing pain which sometimes woke her in the morning as a thing .to be withstoed. She saw that there was something. wrong which defeated her high ideal, but it eluded her when she attempted to inspect it, and she turned from it with a shudder.

FOREIGN NEWS.

THE EAST AFRICAN BLOCKADE.—CRUSH. ING OUT SLAVE-TRADING. VrIONN'A, SIINDAV.—The Austrian Foreign Office has sent a communication to the Austro.Tiungarian Lloyd Company with reference to the blockade of the Fast African coast, in which the company's attention is called to the fact that to prevent the transport of slaves no natives are to be received on board their vessels without certificates. The company is also warned not to carry firearms to the territory against which the blockade is to be directed. ZANZIBAR, SIINDAY.—Thrae. Arab caravans with slaves and ivory are reported to have fought their way into Ballamevo through the opposing coast tribes, being driven by stress of hunger. The Germans then armed these Unyamwese porters with hreech.loading rifles, and sent them back to fight the tribes again. The coast tribes have dug rifle pits along the coast line to protect themselves from the Gteman shell fire. The German attack on Saarlani last Thursday resulted in the cori. plate closure of that route to the interior, and the mis- aionary mails for the interior stations were all sent back to-day. Two Germans left Mnwartwa on the same data as Dr. Bruen'a party, and hare since been unheard of, snd it is feared that they have perished. SENTENCE ON ZULU CHIEFS. DURBAN, SONDAT.—The trial at. Etshowe of Somke :and four other Zulu chiefs on a charge of high treason, rebellion, and public violence has resulted in the prisoners being found guilty on the last count, and -condemned to five years' hard labour. All the accused protested against the sentence, delaring that they had already paid a heavy fine on account of their recent nettle raiding offence. HORRIBLE TRAGEDY NEAR ROME. ...MN, MONDAY EVRNING.—A horrible crime, resem- bling in some respects those perpetrated in the East End •of London, is reported from the neighbourhood of Marino, not far from Rome. A scoundrel named Deceaaris, who enjoys the repwat ion of having sojourned at one time or another in all the prisons of the kingdom, ,allured his niece, Assunta liiordatii, aged 11 years, into a vineyard, and there cut her throat. The rascal told his wife that he had just stabbed a man with whom he 'bad been drinking, and that he must fly for his life. The 'police are now looking for him. SUICIDES AT NIAGARA, • Nearly every suicide at Niagara FaVs leads to others in the same place. The other day a stranger threw hi:nisei! :over the bridge that leads to Goat Island, and was in- -atantly carried over the Falls. His clothes were stripped from him, and when he was disc Yered. two hours after- wards, his corpse was found nakedovhile nearly every bone in his body was broken. Not long afterwards an Englishman, who was identified as Fred Barber, Chip- 16a:use-road, Sheffield, shot himself on the Suspension It was further discovered that he was a Dis- senting minister who arrived recently with a newly. married wife.

REPORTED NEWS FROM MR. STANLEY. The British and African steamer Cameroon (S. Turnbull .00tamander) arrived in the Mersey on Saturday morn- ing. with mails and passengers from the West and South- West Coasts of Africa. According to information brought from Bonny by the Cameroon, a most extra- ordinary rumour was in circulation respecting Mr. H. IL Stanley, the African explorer. The runtour is said to have comet from the river Niger, and was to the effect that Stanley, with a strong armed force, was at the back of the great oil rivers, including the Niger, and was annexing the country. It was said that he was planting the British Bag as he went along, and it was understood that he found the natives very anxious to COMO under the protection of England. The report was said to be brought down the river Niger by the interior natives, who appeared anxious to spread the report. The opinion has been prevalent for years past that the Upper Niger could be reached both from the Congo, on the south side, and from the Senegal, on the north; but beyond the re- port from the Niger, via Bonny, nothing further was gleaned of Mr. Stanley's movements.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

Mr. Sexton has consented to accept the Lord Mayoralty of Dublin. 'The Parnell defence fund now amounts to nearly 223,000. The Irish party, at a meeting in the House of Corn. MOM on Saturday, passed a vote of condolence with Mn. PS'ne on the death of her husband. Dr. Tanner, M.P., and Mr. Carew. M.P., held meetings in Kildare, on sunday, advocating the Plan of Campaign The police arrived after the meetings had closed. Lord Digby's tenants, in King's county, are paying their rents in large numbers; the non-judicial tenants receiving 10 per cent, reduction, and the judicial tenants the Land Commission scale. Mr. Daniel O'Connor, Town Commisioner of Killarney who was sentenced on Wednesday last to six month-s' imprisonment for taking part in the p!an of Campaign On the Kenmare estate, was released from Tr:tire gaol on haturday by order of the Lord Lieutenant, owing, it is supposed, to the feeble state of his health. At a meeting of the Cork Corporation, on Saturday, Alderman Ryan (moderate Nationalist) was elected Mayor for the ensuing year. The election has caused a severe strain in Nationalist circles, as Alderman Horgan, who was defeated by two to one, was the nominee a the Committee of the Cork National League, the strongest branch of the League in Ireland. Mr. Horgan belongs to the extreme, or Gaelic wing. of the party, and the elec- tion of Alderman Ryan is taken as a crushing blow to the " young blood" of the Nationalist movement, who are opposed to clerical interference with politics. ' On Sunday, one of the Waterford fife and drum bands, accompanied by a banner bearing the words, " Remem• ber the Martyrs" on one side, and a large black cross on the other, was parading the streets of the city, when a body of policemen stopped the procession. The crowd relented this, and an encounter between the people and police ensued. The mob hone I a volley of stones at the police, who retaliated by using their batons freely. Several persons were batoned, and several police struck with stories. The police proceeded to clear Michael. street and Broad-street, and on Tu:stay evening the city remained in a very excited state. IN PRISON TWO TEARS FOR REFUSING TO ANSWER

On Tuesday, Serjeant Hemphill applied, in the Dublin Bankruptcy Court, to Judge Boyd, to release Tom Moroney, imprisoned nearly two years ago for refusing to be sworn as a bankrupt, relying on the tendency of the Legislature to abolish imprisonment for debt, and ekelimited terms of imprisonment imposed by tht fudges for contempt. Mr. Gerrard, Q.C., for the assignees, pointed out that the application was made not ad viisericordiam, but to have Moroney discharged as of right: and that Moroney stated that he had subscribed to the Plan of Campaign "war chest," and cleared his land of cattle and effects to defeat the landlord's claim for his rent, £Bs.—Judge Boyd regretted to refuse the application, stating that Moroney could obtain his discharge any moment he =to be sworn, or tha- it appeared he suffered in or body by imprisonment.

VERDICT OF A WELL-KNOWN AUTHOR. _ _

The Rev. Bailey J. Harker, of Bolton, Lancashire, author of "Rambles in Upper Wharfedale;' " Philip Neville, of Garriton," and other works, writes as follows: "For many years I have been in very indifferent health, crippling me in my public duties A a minister, and interfering with my literary -nuts. Fora long time I seemed to suffer chiefly t a nervous affection, and from valvular disease .0 the heart, and was under the necessity, fourteen years ago, of retiring for two years into the country for the benefit of bracing air, rest and quietude. After resuming work, however, at the end of that period, though much improved, I was still far from strong, and my memory was considerably impaired. Life under such conditions was almost unbearable. One day one of your books 'came into my possession, and after reading it I deter- mined to try Warners SIFE Cure.' On the second day after taking the medicine, I became exceedingly worse, but thinking it was owing to the effective action of the remedy, I persevered, and on the third day was surprised to find a great change for the better,and by the time I had finished a few bottles the pain had ceased, the swelling had gone, the veins were reduced to their proper size, • and all the discolourment had disappeared from the skin. Strength came back into my legs and feet, and I felt myself another man." Warner's Sent: Cure can be had at all Chemists and Medicine Vendors in the United Kingdom at 4s. 6d. per :bottle, or of 11. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—SArcituaT. The Speaker took the emir at 12 15. A SCENE.—MR. C. GRAHAM ASKED TO RI7IIHE. There was one quoit-ion on the paper in the name or Mr. C. Graham. respecting the condition of the Cradlev Heath chainmakers, and the First Lord was requested to say if he would afford facilities for a discussion upon A motion connected with the matter standing on the,

paper. Mr. Slurn's answer was that the subject was receiv- ing the earnest attention of the Government, but he could not offer to give facilities for a dehate upon this particular motion, whereupon Mr. Gnsrism, with elabo- rate politeness, reminded the right hon. gentleman the the motion had been set down by one of the supporters of the Government, and suggested that on that account, at least, it was entitled to consideration. Mr. t..4m.trit evinced no disposition to oblige Mr. Graham. who then, in an excited manner, accused the First Lord of committing a "dishonourable trick." The exclama- tion, of course, drew forth loud cries of "Order" from the Ministerialists: and the .Ser.titart, too, was heard asking loudly for order. Rising, he said, "Order, order. the hon, gentleman is behaving in a most unparliamen- tary manner." A number of members on the Minis- terial benches shouted " Withdraw, withdraw "; but Mr. GRAHAM was not penitent, and simply replied that, , be never withdrew when he had said a thing that iv

meant. The Sessesn, addressing himself to Mr. Graham, said " I must ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw. His ex premien is unparliamentary." After Mr. Graham had left the House, the formal motion subjecting to-day's sittings to the rules regu- lating those of Wednesdays was carried without chal- lenge, and, to the surprise of everybody, and especially of Mr. Graham, who could he seen awaltine events out- side the doors below the Bar, Mr. Speaker left the chair. Mr. Courtney came to the table, and the House went directly into Committee of Supply, without ravine taken any further stop in regard to the exciting incident which had just transpired. SUPPLY.—THE POSITION AT SUAKIM. In Supply, on the vote for embassies and missions abroad, Mr. Jouw Montev directed attention te, the operations at Suakim, condemning them as purposeless : and mischievous. He advised that. the Government should abandon Suakin) altogether, or else make a really serious attempt to suppress the slave trade, and Intro- duce civilisation into the Soudan. Sir James FERMISON, in the course of his reply for the Government, said that the British policy at Suakin) was essentially defensive. Although the Egyptian army had been increased it would entail no greater burden on the people. He contended that the British efforts towards the suppression of the slave trade had met with en- couriseing succese, and expressed the hope that nothin,s, would be likely to interfere with the operation. Mr. Joins MORLEY moved to reduce the vote by £5OO. After further discussion, the WAR tSECRWEARY ex- plained the condition of affairs at Suakim, and declared that it was not the intention of the Government to attempt the reconquest of the Eastern Soudan. Theii purpose was to raise the siege of Suakim. and to enable the town to hold its own position in the twee., without the presence and assiatance of English troops and ships. It was impossible to withdraw at once from Suakin). Mr. LADOUCTIRRE protested against the use ni British troops at Suakim. Lord R. CRLECRIT.T, had yet to learn that Egypt proper had any interest in Suakim, and he protested against the doctrine that the holding it against the Soudanese was to fall upon Egyptian revenue. He was afraid that the despatch of a detachment of British in- fantry to reinforce the native troops would lead to a repetition of what. had occurred in the past. Mr. W. H. Sierra said the policy of the Government with regard to Egypt was set out clearly in the conven- tion we endeavoured to enter into with the Porte, viz.. thetas soon as there was adequate security for the peace of Egypt the Government desired to withdraw, and there had been no departure from that policy. The Govern• reent believed they would succeed in building up in Egypt a self-governing empire, capable of resisting an) attacks which might be made upon it by hostile tribes. On a division there were— For the reduction lOl Against Progress was reported shortly afterwards. The report of Supply was agreed to, and the House adjourned at 6 30 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The SOLICITOR-GENERAL for IRELAND stated that, OR the 30th November, last year, there were 64,000 applications for judicial rents undisposed of by the Land Courts ir Ireland. At the same date this year the number was 80,300. The Bows SECRETARY announced, amid cheers, that e free pardon had been granted to the men Brannaghan and Murphy. who were convicted and sentenced to penal servitude for the Edlington Vicarage burglary, in 1879, and who had since been released on proof of theli innocence, and that the Treasury had granted to then. compensation atnounting to £BOO each. SUPPLY.—THE IRISH ESTIMATES. - - - •

The House then went into Committee on the Irisl. Estimates. Criticism arose on the political leanings of tho Lord-Lieutenant, on the payment of his State officers, and on the preeent distribution ot Queen's Plates. When the vote of £12,707 for the Chief Secretary's salary and expenses was reached, Mr. J. ELLIS moved its reduction by £425, and spoke with considerable irony of the Chief Secretary's Lodge in Phcenix Park. No one, he said amid laughter, occu- pying the position of Mr. Balfour had had less occasion for fuel there, and therefore he wished to istrike off that item. The vote raised the whole policy of the Govern- ment in Ireland, and he held that the Chief Secretary's policy had been one of brutality, concealment, and evasion. Mr. Bervonn replied with some warmth. Mr. Guterrornt followed, and in a powerful speech. brushed away Mr. Balfour. He diselaimed any inten- tion ef attributing to the Chief Secretary personal responsibility for his Irish policy, which, he said, he threw upon the Cabinet in its collective capacity. ne severely condemned the personal attacks Mr. Balfour made upon himself and othcrs. Especially he censured his allusions to Lord Spencer's connection with the imprisonment of Mr. T. Harrington under the late Government, and taunted him with repeating his charges by additional untrue statements instead of offering the apology to Lord Spencer to which he insisted he was entitled. Touching upon the circumstances connected with the murder of Kinsella and the imprison- ment of Mr. Mandeville which he characterised as shocking and brutal,—he referred to them to show the utter apathy of the Government where injury was done to Irishmen who belonged to the National party. Ha next rehearsed the details connected , with the Mitchelstown riot, contending that the action of 1 the police was/ eltogether unjustifiable, and enlarged upon the gross injUstice done to the Irish people by the incompetence of some of the resident magistrates. In Ireland the ministers of law and order trampled law and order under foot. Of all the delusions ever attempted to be practised in the country the grossest and least warrantable was this—that the administration of the law which now prevailed in Ireland was an honourable, pure, or just administration, or that the Government who supported it were champions of law and order. Mr. A. J. BALFOrrt explained that for his error at Glasgow about the treatment of the member for Dublin, he had apologised to Lord Spencer. Tfe defended the trial of Kinsella's murderer. Mandeville's death had nothing to do with his treatment in prison. Observing Mr. Gladstone leaving the House, Mr. Balfour remarked that the right hon, gentleman preferred to make accu- sations to listening to debate. He supported and ap- proved Dr. Barr's action, and said the action of the police at Mitchelstown was perfectly legal. Mr. Glad- stone having returned to hie place Mr. Balfour, con- tinuing, said ho could not plead guilty to evading diffi- culties or shirking disagreeable points. Often as these things were refuted, the Opposition still depended on the old dishes, cooked and re-cooked, and served up time after time, till he should have thought that those who cheered most loudly were sickened and nauseated. After speeches from Mr, Flynn, Mr. A. Pease, and Mr. Waddy, Mr. Dit.tom dwelt upon the unfair and partisan spirit in which the law was adtninistered in Ireland, and charged the Government with aiding and abetting the improper acquittal of loyalists charged with crime. Sir G. TRINELYAN, detailing the circumstances attend- ing the relaxation of the prison rules in favour of Mr. T. Harrington, contended that Lord Spencer acted in strict accordance with the law and the prison rules, and pointed out that Lord Spencer's version of the affair was a direct contradiction or Mr. Balfour's statement Mr. A. J. 11.sr.vozin persisted in his content ion that Lord Spencer had acted illegally and Irregularly in regard to Mr. Harrington. The debate was adjourned, and the House adjourned at 1 10.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUFSDAY. Ti 0-ATRS B 1 LL PASSIM—The Oaths Bill was reaa a third time.—On the motion that the bill do pass, 1,,,rd FITZGERALD moved that the words "no religious belief " should be expunged, and the words "contrary to his re- ligious belief or moral convictions" SPENCER opposed Lord Fitzgerald's amendment, on the ground that it would unsettle the compromise arrived at in the House of Commons.—The amendment was rejected, and the bill passed. THE IRISH LAND PURCHASE BILL. Lord ASHROURNE moved the second reading of the Land Purchase (Ireland) Bill, authorising further loans to the extent of £5,000.000. Earl Aberdeen and Earl Spencer, whilst agreeing with the principle of the Land Purchase Bill, objected that it did not deal with arrears, was not sufficiently compre- hensive, and that repayments were not properly secured. Earl Milltown, Earl Camperdown, and Earl Derby supported the bill, because it was sound in principle, and would do more to pacify Ireland than any other measure which the Government could bring forward. Lord DENMAN livoved the rejection of the bill, but it was read a second time without further discussion.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 3 30 p.m. QUES [IONS.
Mr. W. H. BMITH, in —answer- to Mr. Jas. Stevenson, said he hoped that the second reading of the Sunday Closing

Bill might be taken on Friday evening, the 14th inst.— Mr. Sravaxsow, however, said that it was not is accord- ance with his view of the discharge of his duty to ac- cept so late a date for the second reading of his bilL Mr. SMITH offered to give attention to the question of changing the Christmas Bank Holiday from Wednesday

to Monday. THE DESPATCH OF TROOPS TO SUAKIM.—MOTION BY LORD It CHURCHILL. Lord Rartnotru CHURCTITLL had an important ques- tion on the paper, and, receiving no satisfactory answer, intimated that he felt it his duty to move the adjourn- ment of the House. The question of the noble lord was whether the military atithorities at the headquarter, at home were consulted before it was decided by the Government to send a British battalion v. Suakini. and whether they approved of the policy, of dispatching so slender a reinforcement of British troops.—The answer of Mr. STANUOPIR was to the . effect that the Government acted on their own responsi- bility in the matter. The local military authorities originally intended to undertake the operation, but, the amount. of British force now sent was that. asked for in consequence of the offer of the British Government. It was thought ample for the purpose, but he had tele- graphed some inquiries after representations from his military advisers.--Shortly afterwards. Lord R. Cuouctritt, supported by the Opposition. rose to move the adjournment of the House, in order to discuss the dispatch of British troops to Suakim. The noble lord said the object of his motion WWI to prev,--nt the employment of British troops in aerious enterprises in the Soudan. until further information had been offered to the House concerning the method and the means of their service. Ile believed the gwates military authorities were opposed to the step taken 13) the Government. and he urged the House to interfere

before mischief Was done. ." Sir L. Prr.ty seconded the adjournment. Mr. Svaxtiors defended the action of the Government The noble lord had said the policy of the Government was not good, but he insisted the noble lord had come to that conclusion, without being in posses.sion of facts to warrant the assertion. Col. Nolan and General Goldsworthy criticised the policy of the Government. Sir W. TIAIRCOVRT dbsired to know when the decision to embark on the operations was arrived at. Mr. E. STA:more said the decision was come to last Tuesday. After some further discussion, Mr. fltanvroms said he was not prepared to vote azainst the motion of the nobls lord. Lord Tlartington, on the contrary, voted against it. On a division there were— For the adjournment Against SUPPLY.—THE TREATMENT OF TRlsr{ POLITICAL
