Dundee bae been elevated to the po4itlon of a city. Waddle, the Durham murderer, will be hanged on

December 17th. The ship Inch Murren. fmm Iquique to Pit }mouth, has been abandoned at sea, having caught fire. Mr. Monro, the new Metropolitan. Police Commie. sioner, assumed his new duties on Monday. - A disastrous firs occurred at South. Durham- Salt Works, near Middlesbrough, on Monday, resllting in genet damage to buildings. ' Three men have been arrested at Kelso, suspected of being concerned in the death of,. man named Miller whose body was recovered from the Tweed. Saturday heing the 44th anni resery of thebir bof the Princess of Wales, the occasion s :narked by the ring- ing a the church bells at, Win so and. St. James's, and the firlaz of royal salutes. *1 eta rams of conp.,ratula- lions were wilt from Windsor Ce..tle and Cuinberland Lodge. The Duke of Devonshire has oftered to the town 0, Buxton four and a half acres of land, worth £3,000, called the Serpentine, for a park, on condition that the Local Beard keep it in order; and s.lso 3,660 yards of land, worth about £l,OOO, in connection with the new

Town Hall. ;Another great fire OCCUTted it& Glasgow, on Tuesday .ienr the scene of last wets's cAittagrat ion. A large pro- vision warehouse, of four esoreys. in Fox-street, belong- ing to Mr. George Dictsoze was destroyed, the damage being estimated at £lO,OOO. The street being narrow, the fire brigade were much hampered in their endeavours to extinguish the flamed. Tux Rtrostarric Rialto-rt.—The Bishop of Lincoln, in a letter to the clergy and laity of his diocese on the sub. ject of his prosecution for Ritualistic practices, main- tains that the Ornaments Rubric sufficiently oovers the principle of ritual contended for. Ile could not admit the charge of law-breeking, and repudiates with Indig- nation the imputation of disloyalty either to England or _ .

the English Church. FATAL AOCIDWri AT • AOLTOK SPINNIWiI On Saturday, a shocking accident occurred at Messrs. Crosses and Winkworth's No. 5 Spinning Mill, Bolton. A card tenter, named Alice Isherwood, was caught by a strap whilst at work, and had her skull fractured by being dashed to the ground, death resulting almost im- mediately. The deceased had only been engaged since Friday, and is 22 years old. Intim= af KiNDAL.—An inquest was held at Kendal. on Monday, by Mr. J. Wilson, coroner, on the body of a widow, named Mrs. Mary Scott, 68, a Highgate, who had died on Saturday evening. The deceased was on the New Bead with some friends on the evening of the 10th November, witnessing the pleasure fair, when a man (unknown), who was riding by, knocked her down. she was carried home, and death ensued to concussion of the brain.
t 25th

FATALITIES AT WIGAN.—TWO mill girls, named Berry, whilst walking from Newton to W igen, on Saturday, te their work, fell into the river Douglas. One sister managed to scramble out, but the other was drowned. The morning was very dark and foggy. A shunter, named James Lambert, whilst working in the Lancashire and Yorkshire goods yard, Wigan, early on Saturday, was somehow caught between the wag- gons and killed. CACTITON TO FlowTrits.—At Leamington Police Court. on Monday morning. Henry Smith. printer and stationer, of London and Leaminetem, was fined £2O and costa for issuing a placard reflecting on the character o/ one of the candidates at the recent municipal elections at. Leamington without acpendin,g the name of the printer and publisher to it. This is the first prosecution of the kind under the Municipal Elections Corrupt and Illegal Practices Act, 1864. IteronrED Loss or TERRE LIVES BY FlRP..—Consider- able excitement has been caused at Apedale, North Staf- fordshire, by the report that three men have perished in the recent fire at the farm of Mr. Gardiner in that village. The men in question, who've absence has only now been noticed, were seen on the burnt-out premises on the night of the fire, and it is conjectured that they fell victims to the flames whilst they were asleep. A search is being made for their bodies. FORGED STLVIIR ConSS.—lt has tranmire 1 that a large amount of forged silver coins, estimate tat about £95,090 out of a total currency in that metal in the United Kingdom of £20,000,000, Is now in the hands of the public. These coins, which impartially range from threepence up to half-a-crown nmece, cannot be called spurious, for they are made of good metal; but bar silver has fallen during the past two years about 4d. per ounce, and hence there+ is a large profit on these transactions, ranging, it is cilculated, from 50 to 70 per cent. HORRIBLE Mrraina Bi A Somme—intelligence re- ceived on Monday states that a frightful tragedy wa.s committed in the married quarters of the S Battery Ist Brigade Royal Artillery. stationed at Bellary. Madras, on the Bth ult. Corporal Hardwick was engaged in shaving when he began an altercation With his wife, and in a fit of desperation he literally hacked off her head with his razor. The murderer gave himself up immediately, and at the inquest a verdict of wilful murder was returned against him. The terrible affair cast a gloom over the whole garrison. A ROXANTIC AFFAIR NEAR KIDDERMINSTER. A iomantic affair which has occurred not far from the _ carpet metropolis has caused some excitement in the neighbourhood. A.Young lady of good family having formed an acquaintance with the young, gardener of a neighbouring squire, an sttachment appears to have sprung up between them, which culminated a few days ago in the gardener taking train tor a distant city, to be follgwal in a- few days by the young lady; and it is now riorfeil that the Couple have been married. The young lady is possessed of considerable wealth, and her family is well knownin the ceanty, Citeeekritto A RlTVOLllrtoti.—the bicentenary of the Revolution of 1888 was celebrated on Monday at White tington and Chesterfield with considerable festivity. The Revolution House, which has been presented to the people by its former owners as a national memorial, was on view. There was service in the local churches, a procession, loyal speeches, a banquet, and a display of fireworks. The old cottage in which tile first Duke of Devonshire and the other plotters met for the overthrow of Ring James H. is to he- thoroughly restored, and so enthusiastic are the inhabitants of East Derbyshire shout the time-worn historic house that there will be little difficulty in getting funds to keep it in repair. Atansileo Teistwav Accltieter.—On Saturday morn- ing, two steam tramcars collided while proceeding is opposite directions on the Leeds-r.ad tram line, Brad- ford. The driver of one of the care, which was pro- ceeding down an incline in the direction of the town, was unable to pull up at a crossing, owing to the slip. neriness of the rails, and the up-co:flino car was thrown off the line by the collision. Many of the pawners, of whom there was a large number, were severely shaken, And a driver had two ribs fractured. With the excep- tion of the driver and a lady passenger, the occupants of the cars were able to proceed. Traffic was delayed tor about half an hour. MRS. LANGTRY'S DIVORCE STMT.—Mrs. Langtry ap- pears to have some trouble in obtaining her American livorce. She recently took up her residence in Rhode Island for the purpose of facilitating her separation from her husband. It appears that the suit will he opposed by Mr. Langtry, who receatly visited New York under the name of Leslie for the purpose of opposing the divorce. A friend of his, in ap.aakinz of the -case, said: "If Mrs. Langtry brings her suit, her husband will de- fend his character to the last" It, is further stated in this connection that Mr. Langtry hal received certain suggestions for compromise from Mrs. LA ngt ry's lawyers, and that these propositions had been rerctetl. She is about to appear as Lady Macbeth. Mr. Chas. Coghlan will play Macbeth. ALARMING R A TLWA Y A CMDENT.—A serious railway collision occurred on Saturday • evening on the London and North-Western Railway, just outside Manchester. A :low train was leaving London-road Station for Cheadle. The weather was liaav, and the signals could not readily be observed. Wien the engine got clear of the platform the driver saw it train crossing the points. This proved to be the slow train from Sti-ickport. The driver applied the brake, 1t..; 000ld not pull up his train. and the engine struck the incoming train on the broadside, about the second or third carriage from the engine. Three car- riages were smashed to pieces, and the engine was knocked off the line. The front of the outgoing engine was damaged, but it maintained its position on the tine. A number of passengers were injurel, and six of the more serious cases were conveyed to the Infirmary. Traffic was blocked for about two hours. INTEMPERANCE CkrEED. —A wealthy American Lady whose only son was fcr years a slave to intemperance, after seeking In vale for a cure, and trying all known remedies, at last found a simple means that cured and save him from a drun- kard's grave. Anyone suffering or desiring to help others in this worthy muse, by sending a self-addressed stamped en- velope to Mr. James Holland, 25, Hart-st., High Holborn, London, will receive this information free of charge. Men- tion this paper.—Adet. VESSEL BURNT AT SKl.—The crew of the British barque Sutherfield were landed at Plymouth on Thurs- day morning, their vessel having been burnt at sea. After the outbreak of the fire she had to be almost immediately abandoned, and soon afterwards foundered. Her crew were picked up by the Liverpool ship Adventurer. ART CONGRESSIN LIVERPOOL.—On Monday evening the first Congress of the National Association for the Ad- vancement of Art said its Application to Industry was inaugurated at St. George's Hall, Liverpool. ' Sir Frederick Leighton, Bart., P.R.A. delivered the presi- dential address,' in the course of which he referred to the present and future position of art in England, pointedly showing the cause and need there was for the associa- tion which Was being inaugurated. On Tuesday the Congress commenced its sectional meetings. In the evening the Mayor gave a banquet to Sir F. Leighton, Bart. On Wednesday papers were read by Mr. Walters Crane, Mr. Holman Hunt, Mi. Wm. Morris, and other well-known workers in the art world. There was also a discussion on the Sunday opening of art galleries. On Thursday the Congress decided to accept a warm invitation to hold its meeting next year at Edinburgh. The president of the Royal Scottish Academy was appointed to succeed Sir Frederick Leighton at the head of the Association.

div.head: PRISONERS.
div.p: PRISONERS.

In Committee of Supply, the debate was resumed on Mr. John Ellie's motion to reduce tbe vote for the ese pensee and salaries of the Chief Secretary for Ireland's office. Mr. W. O'BRIEN reverted to the circumstances in con- nection with the imprieonment of Mr. John Mandeville, and contended that the unfortunate man was done to death by seven armed gaolers, for whose tectien lie in. slated the ‘-, Secretary was pri merits- reeponsible. fie severely se ed the ac ion ot Dr. Parr, eeee came from this country .0 flog Dr. Ridley up to his work. Mr. A. J. BAT.POUn replied to the charges of iehumanity as regarded the trratmert of Mr. Mandeville In prison. The right hon. gentleman was so frequently interrupted hy lush members as to call for reproof from the Chair- man. Coming to the charge of Mr. Mendeville being left In his cell, shivering without his elements, Mr. Pet- rone said the ReCtISEIiOn WAS a ridiculous fiction. As te Mr. Mandeville's death, the weight of medical evidence she wed the disease of which he died Was not contracted vrtele in prison. Ti' insisted the whole of the charges brought against him as to inhuman treatment of pob- I prisoners had failed, and .he left. the controversy with safety to the judgment of the country. Mr. T. P. O'Coseort insisted that prison torture was the eawe of Mr. Mandeville's death. Mr. H. Wiesow, from personal observation regarding the affray at Mitcheletown, said it Was ridiculous to say the barracks was in danger when the firing took place. He insisted it Was quite possible to shoot, Loner- inn at the spot where lie fell by point blank, and not a ricochet shot. He further said he had photograglied the barracks from the place where Lonerean fejt, and the result proved incontestably that the theory of the Chief Secretary was wrong, and that the man was killed by a direct shot from the barracks. Sir W. HattcounT denied ha had ever led Lord Spencer astray with regard to prison discipline as the Chief Secretary stated on Monday night. The assertions of the Chief Secretary with reference to prison dis- cipline were in doctrine unsound, and uncon- stitutional, and in all his etatements of facts on the subject he had been proved to be in- accurate. The Lord-Lieutenant and Chief Secretary were absolutely responsible to Parliament for what WAS done in prise tie, and to set up the independent authority of the Prison Board was an unconstitutional doctrine put forward to shelter the Chief Secretary from respori- eibility. He insisted there ought to be a searching in- dependent public inquiry, to ascertain whether the police were justified its firing on the people at Mitchels- town. Mr. A. J. Beeroce defended himself from the accuse- tions of Sir W. Harcourt. end pointed out that during Mr Gladstone's administration many lives had been lost, and in no instance had public inquiry ever taken place. Mr. JOHN MORLEY strenuously demanded the inquiry asked for.—Mr. PARNELL contended that sentence* more severe than the nature of the case required had been inflicted on political prisoners by the present Irish Executive. The proposed reduction was rejected by 233 to 181, and the vote was agreed to. The House adjourned at 12 45 a.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter past twelve o'clock. THE NEW WIMBLEDON.—Mr. STANHOPE in reply to Sir , John Swinburne, said he could not give an undertaking not to enter into a definite arrangement for granting 1, any right of user over any Crown lands for the pur- I pose of the requirements of the National Rifle Associa- tion until an opportunity had been afforded for discuss- ing the principle of such concessions. He would be 'prepared to state the views of the Government when the subject was raised on the Army Estimates. The House would, whenever a rote was presented to the House for any such purpose, have an opportunity of expressing an opinion upon it. SUPPLY.—The Houseethen went into Committee of Supply on the Irish Estimates. After a brief discussion a vote of £554 for the office of the Comnsissioner of ICharitable Funds and Bequests was agreed to. On the vote of £61,698 for the Local Government Board in Ireland, Mr. Haety raised a discussion, in which a num- ber of members took part. SAND GROUSE.—The Sand Grouse Protection Bill was read a second time. The House adjourned at half-past six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS, THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Irish Land Purchase Bill was , passed through Committee with only one amendment— accepted by Lord Asitesounsree—and was also read a third time. The Municipal Funds (Ireland) Bill, the Public Health Acts Amendment (Buildings in Stree'.,s) Bill, and the Sea Fisheries Regulation Bill were read a third time and passed. Their Lordships adjourned at ten minutes past six o'clock till fuesday next. HOUSE OF COMMONS, THURSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock. Quesetenes.—Mr. MACLEAN put a question about Lord Dufferin's recent speech in Calcutta, and was informed by Sir JOHN GORST that it was a factthat representations had been made to the Government of India by native chiefs and leading Mahometans as to the mischievous effect of the publications of the Indian National Con- gress and the speeches made by delegates Wile Congress. Mr. STANHOPE informed Mr. John Morley that General Dormer had in answer to his (Mr. STANHOPR',4) telegram repeated his former assurance as to the completely satis- factory character of the military force sent to Suakim. PUBLIC BUSINESS, &c.—Mr. LABOUCHEIIE moved the adjournment of the House in order to call at- tention to the unsatisfactory state of pub- lic business. Mr. Saturn attributed the condition of things to the protracted discussions in Committee of Supply on matters of grievance, and‘said that next session the Government would see that the Civil Service Estimates were taken at an early period, and were got through without the pressure which had been expe- rienced this session. After some discussion, Mr. LABOUCHERE withdrew his motion, his object in bringing it forward having been fulfilled. The usual motion for the suspension of the twelve o'clock rule was then carried, and the House again went into Committee of Supply on the Irish Estimates.

MILL FIRE AT FRFSTON.—EarIy on Thursday morning, a fire broke out in the preparing department of the Smillbrook Mill, of Messrs Hampson and Fish. The fire brigade was summoned, and after working some time extinguished the flames. The shed is not seriously damaged. The damage amounts to about £l,OOO SHOCKING QUARRY ACCIDENT.—A distressing fatality was reported to the Leicestershire Coroner on Thursday. It appears that during operations at the Bardon Hill Granite Quarries a large mass sf stone fell, and a man named James Henson was buried underneath it. Death was found to be instanteous, his spine having been broken. The deceased leaves a wife and eight children. TERRIFIC GAS EXPLOSION.—A terrific gas explosion occurred at Bradford on Thursday morning, on the extensive spinning and manufacturing premises of Mitchell Bros. The workpeople were just commencing for the day, and a man named Joseph Priestley, employed in the carding-room, had lit up, when he noticed a strong smell of gas proceeding from the room below. He was proceeding to enter the room, when a terrific explosion took place. The doors of the rooms were blown out in his face, and he was knocked down and rendered insensible. Another man who had just entered the ground floor rooms lamed Rufus Clough, was also severely burnt and bAsed. The windows of the ground floor storey, of thick glass, were blown to atoms, and the flooring of the first storey was broken through, heavy flagstones lifted out of their places, and masonry wrecked. A man named Rouse, who was passing the mill, was badly hurt by fragments of glass ' and masonry. Priestley is in a critical condition.

Ile would m.k the GovernMent, who had given 'five millions to pay Irish landlords, to assist them. Mr. Graham's reception was most enthusiastic, DEATH OF A MEMBER' OF PARLIAMENT.

Major Alexander Henry Rote. member for Maidstone, died suddenly in London, onTisesday, from heart disease. So well was the hon. member ,is the morning that at 11. o'clock lie was at the Carlton Club. Deceased was born in 1829. He was educated at Eton and Christ Church, Oxford, graduated M.A. in 11th, and was miled to the Bar at the Inner Templet in, 185%. In 1874 he was an unsuccessful candidate foe Maidstone as Conservative, but WAS returned in 1880, and has since sat for the con- stituency. About mid-day be WAS found reclining in a chair in his sitting-room apparently lifeless. Dr. Broad- bent, cf Seymour-street. his medical adviser, was at once sent for, and pronounce I the Major deal, the cause assigned being heart disease. The deceased had been unwell for some Hine. and had decided upon making a trip to the South of France. Mr. John Barker, of Kensington, has been invited to become the Gladstonian candidate for Maidstone. He is the partner of Lord Mayor Whitehead.

div.head: LONDON OUTRAGES.
div.p: THE LONDON OUTRAGES.

Letters signed "Jack the Ripper" continue to be received by the metropolitan police, and another was received by Mr. Saunders. Thames Police Court magise trate, on Monday, from Wellingborough. containing idle threats. In Boston the Whitechepel fiend has been imitated by a man who hides in dark corners and darts oa at women, brandishing a knife and muttering threats. He is undoubtedly insane. and the police are "arresting him numerously." Another outcome of the Whitechapel horror is a Chinese ghost, with the face of a dragon, which appears in Pell-street, in the Chinese quarter, and friehtens women. It is reported by cable from Eurrtp• that, a certain person, whose name is known, has s4iled from Havre for New York, who is famous for his hatred of women, and who has repeatedly made threats against females of dissolute character. ALLEGED ATTACK ON ANOTHER WOMAN. Great excitement was caused, early on Monday morn- in, in the neighbourhood of Ring's Crees, London, by the report of an attempt to murder a woman in a street off Etiston-road. The victim of the outrage ' was Harriet North, 35, living at 13, Wood-street, Cromer- street, Gray's Inn-r,-'ad. She was accosted, about one o'clock, in Euston-road, opposite the Midland Grand Hotel, by a man, apparently a foreigner, and she accompanied him into Belgrave-street, towards Argyle-square. She states that he made seine accusa- tion against her, and she then felt a blow from a sharp instrument in the abdomen. She called out "What have you done ! " and her assailant, without saying any- thing more, ran sway. She was too exhausted to follow him, and a female friend, coming up later, alarmed the who took the injured woman to the Royal Free iinspital, Gray's Inn-road, where she was at once ad- mitted. ;North's friend informed the police that she had been previously accosted by tho same man, but, not liking his appearance, she refused to accompany him The woman was examined by two doctors at the hospital and one of them afterwards stated to a reporter that he did not think she had been stabbed, and that at any rate her story was much exaggerated. She admitted this' she did not scream out. The doctor did not think it WAS a ease of premeditated aseault, and believed that ti• man was probably as much alarmed as the woman het self.

div.head: DRUNK PiRD'S FATE.
div.p: A DRUNK PiRD'S FATE.

On Monday afternoon Hf. 8. nrighOuse, Coronef for South-West Lancashire:attended at the Bay Horse Inn, Winwick-st., Warrington, to inquire Into the circumstances of the death of a woman named Ann Ford, who died suddenly on the pre- vious Friday. The deceased, who was about 53 years of age, was rather a notorious character, and was well-known to the police. Drunkenness seems to have been her great failing, and for that offence she made a number of appearances before the magistrates. She earned a living by hawking, and was separated from her husband, who is t carter. For two or three weeks past she had been lodg- ing in Bay Horse yard, and had, according to the evidence adduced, been in a state of drunkenness nearly all that time On Friday evening she was drunk, and was seen loaning against the door of the house where she lodged. Later on her dead body was found on the kitchen floor.—The first witness called was the husband, John Ford, who, after being sworn, said that he had not seen the body of the deceased. The Coroner informed him that it was necessary that he should do so, and after some demur he accompanied a policeman to the house where the body was lying. On his return he said that he identified the body as that of his wife. He had no settled place of abode. Some time ago he lodged , at No. 3, Old Gardens. The deceased was his wife, and ' he believed she was about 52 or 53 years of age. He did not know whether she had been lodging at 7, Bay! Horse-yard, as he had been separated from her for 11 years. The last time he saw her alive was on the 24th October at the Bridewell, when she had him Ipcked up. —Anne Chester, a married woman, said she lived at 7, Bay Horse-yard, and the deceased had lodged with her for the past two or three weeks. She last saw her alive at half-past eight on Friday morning, when witness left home for the day to do some washing. The deceased was then sober She had left a shilling somewhere, and was going to look for it. When witness returned in the evening, about five minutes to nine, she found her house in darkness, and going inside saw the deceased lying on the floor at the bottom of the stairs. She shook her, but receiving no answer, went for a neighbour, and it was found that Mrs. Ford was dead. Deceased's feet were on the lower part of the stairs. Whet' witness had gone away on previous occasions she had locked her house up, but on the day in question the deceased promised to remain sober, and she left the key with her. The deceased had promised witness that she would take the pledge. She (deceased) had been drinking very heavily of late, and had only been sober two nights during the whole of the time 'that she had lodged with witness. She was drunk the night before her death, and that was the reason why she did not know where she had left the shilling that she had lost. The deceased lost the use of her legs when she got drunk.—Margaret Johnson, 1, Grounds-court, said that she had known the deceased very well. She saw her soon after seven o'clock on on Friday evening, at the door of Mrs. Chester's house. Deceased said—" Mrs. Johnson, where are you going to ? Will you have a glass of beer with me ?" Wit- ness replied, "No, you are very ill drunk." The de ceased was drunk. Witness afterwards saw the dead body of the deceased.—lnspector Cox said that at twenty past nine he and Constable Singleton went to Mrs. ehesters' house, where they found the deceased lying on her back with her feet on the bottom step. She was dead. He should think she had been dead for an hour, as her hands were quite cold. There were no blood stains nor marks of violence to be seen. His impression was that while in a state of intoxication she had fallen backwardsagainst the wall, had stunned her- self, and had died whilst in that position. He had known her for the last 16 years. She had been a very heavy drinker. There was no suspicion of foul play. The husband of deceased was at Southport when (the death occurred, and the wonran with whom with whom he cohabited only came out of prison on Saturday morn- ing.—This was all the evidence adduced, and the jury returned a verdict to the effect that death was acci- dental.

Mr. Gladstone arrived at Elawarden on Wednesday night about nine o'clock, looking remarkably well. He attended early prayers at the Parish Church on Thurs- day morning. A telegram from New York reports that a six-inch Bessemer cast steel gun, the first of its kind ever made in America, underwent its first test on Wednesday, and burst under a charge of 481 b. of powder. The widow of Mr. Snell, the Chicago capitalist, who was recently murdered, offers a reward of 50,000dels. for the arrest of-the murderer, in whatever part of the world his apprehension may be effected.

bus is the Season of Fogs,,ivhen,to quote one of Our poets, "the mists and exhalations that now lir% from hill or steaming lake" become, as they
..rig over our large cities, charged with substances Which are irritating and hurtful to humanity. In is noted for many things, and for its fogs
4 much as anythibg else. LOndonfog has been tlerseabed as a "hellish and dismal cloud of sea Coal "; it is "fog phis smoke "—so some of the led say, though .there are others who question
assertion. Mr. THOMAS MORRIS of Warrington
Ag a few years ago on "Smoke and London ;41bglii" advanced quite a different theory. He said

The chief cause of London fog, I venture to say, in the immense vehicular and pedestrian traffic in the streets, cutting up the pathways, leaving a 'dust behind as line as the particles" of moisture, %the latter holding the former mechanically in the 411 r, until a cool still atmosphere condenses the uniidit3r into visible vapour. This in its turn ,tonverts the hitherto dry invisible dust. into a colour that is darker, exactly as the light colou:ed dust of iour streets is converted into black mud by a storm t)f rain.
DODD proceeded to criticise this new Of the subject, and Mr. Moants replying,

Ca-non Dodd thought it was the smoke from domestic Ilrea that caused London fogs to be so thick Ha (Mr. Morris) contended it was fine dust. imovf was it there were not such heavy fogs in -ivaris? His reply was that the dust was kept down IRa frequent and copious use of water, in the ulevards and Champs Elyges in particular. either was the traffic so great as in London. 44 cannot be held that the theory advanced by _

-r• NORMS has made headway, for it does not °over all the facts; but it is due to him to say it is a some degree supported by a valuable Paper Isaned in " Research," for December Ist, from the Pen of Dr. McPherson. The subject is "The Illuneration of Dust-particles in the Air." After 4eBcribing the experiments made to determine the .Iber of dust-particles that are found to be Prganie germs, he proceeds to refer to inorganic (11'st-particles in the following terms : Rut what about the inorganic particles which not be thus propagated and enlarged for easier ~.meteetion ? Mr. John Aitken, F.R.S.E.. of 'Falkirk, ''as counted them. He has enlarged. them by other process to enable him to enumerate them. fte proved, some years ago, that without dust there rn be no fogs, no mist, no rain. He showed this ~"1. forcing common air through a filter of cotton- -7°l into a glass receiver, and injecting steam into closed vessel. There was no appearance of

Batil; there was no fog. When ilie steam is ijected into a glass vessel.containing ordinary air, tile dense cloud is at once observed. Thus, particles Water—vapour require solid bodies on which to orra fog. The fine particles of dust in the air act Its free-surfaces for this purpose. When the dust- ' tarticles are small and numerous, fog is formed; „hen they are larger and fewer, mist or rain is e result. 4-o.r. MORRlS—from whom we have had ft corn- , I.3lunication—regards this passage as demonstrat- , I_l4g the truth of his statement as to London fog ing caused by London dust; but it seems to us 'at it in part only% supports his theory. The ref erred to by Mr. Moaßts is the dust of 'fehicular and pedestrian traffic''; but Dr. 4ePanasoN means that and something more; the *ln-particles ho speaks of are found everywhere; sea as on land; in the deepest mine as well as the highest mountain; in the sweetest of 'ws as well as in the streets of London. It that by "kicking up such a dust "—such - dust—as they do in the metropolis the tants aid the conditions that produce but it is by no means established that m fog is caused solely, or in the main, by m traffic. It is certainly a significant thing in Paris—where, comparatively speaking, coal is used, dense fogs such as punish in London are unknown. The use 'of the v-cart is not, as it seems to:us, sufficient to

exPain the difference. It is more probable that it s because there axe fewer manufactories, and that coke is used for domestic fares: In another ?ortion Of his paper Dr. MoPinxiisow says :-- From numerous experiments made by Mr. Aitken, he is ,able to give the dust-particles in a thousandth part of a cubic inch of the air examined. In outside air the number was 521, when the examination was made after a heavy rain-fall, and 2,119 when the air had been for some time dry. This showS a very marked differenee of four to one, sad this may yet be made available as a test of the sr ate of the atmosphere, as a help to rmeteorological inquiry. In the vitiated air of his room, above 10,000 dust-particles were counted in the thousandth ef a cubic inch. And when he examined the air isinr from the flame of a Bunsen burner, he found tbout 500 millions in a cubic inch. Here we have an enormous increase of chist- pariicles wholly apart from street. traffic. The air, be it -noticed, is vitiated to begin with; there are 33 millions of dust-partici** to the cubic inch; twnt7hTl !..:!Ha. Bunsen lamer, is in Operation there I are not less than 500 millions to the cubic inch. What naturally suggests itself in this connection is whether, and how far,. the consumption of coal in our manufactories and forges acts after the fashion of the Bunsen burner. If it be, as is supposed, that the smoke from domestic and other fires in the metropolis enormously adds to the dust-particles, and that each particle becomes a roe surface for vapour to act upon, we have a more adequate explanation of the cause of fog than that which is presented by the street traffic theory. It is, of course, likely enough that both causes are in operation; but we .cannot forget that the Bunsen burner is a very don.on in producing dust-particles. We Should life to hear what Mr. MORRIS, and others who have given special atten- tion to the subject, have to say on this point; for the question as to how far smoke is a mischief- maker is one which is of vital importance to the community.

In our next issue we purpose giving a striking representation of a mechanical "Grabber "—at work on the Ship Canal.
. Primroses and wallflowers are disporting them- selves in December; they are under the delusion that spring has come. Poor things they will have to suffer for it. The weather is fooling the flowers.

'Viscount Cross has again been "replying to Mr. Gladstone. Happy country that has such a Vicount for ita bulwark! It it hard, to be sure, on Mr. Gladstone; but every man must bear his Cross as best he can.

It is "one for the teetotallers" that Littlewood, the champion pedestrian of the world, has found from a recent test that he can walk better without beer than with it. He speaks as one having authority, and not as the scribes. ,

Lord Salisbury has " come over" on the question of fen' ale suffrage. He says he can conceive no argument by which women are excluded from the exercise of the parliamentary franchise. A movement which has Prime Ministere for converts is certainly progressing.

It is very wrong—quite shocking in fact—for "a Worcestershire young lady of good county family," to marry "a gardener who is reported to be a young man of good looks and good character." Still "nature will have her way," let county families say what they will. And besides, "passing down the train of long descent," there was one Adam, was there not, who Was a gardener?

The Chairman of the Warrington Conservative meeting on Monday evening, in South-west Ward, said he "regretted to see such a small attendance, but it was no donbt owing to the inclement state of the weather, and to various entertainments." Just so; the "entertainments" did it. Conserva- tive meetings are not entertaining.

Alderman Harrison, at the same meeting, had the hardihood to say. that Mr. Balfour'ipolicy had been of "Vie most humane description.' What a travesty of the truth! Why, whilst he was about it, did he not say it was gentle, loving, tender- hearted? It is not denied that whilst the late John Mandeville was suffering from diarrho3a he was put crn punishment diet—bread and water? Would Alderman Harrison think it "humane" if he were treated in a similar fashion?

There was no talk about Mr. Balfour being "humane" when Mr. Gladstone had done with him, in the House of Commonsl on Monday. He held the mirror up to nature in such a way that the Chief Secretary looked hideous. It justified the assertion of Mr. J. Ellis that the administra- tion of Mr. Balfour's policy was "one of petty malignity and calculated brutality." And yet Mr. Gladstone employed .neither abuse nor invective. It was sufficient that he stated the facts, and facts constitute a terrible indictment of the policy of the Chief Secretary.

By way of answer to Lord Salisbury's remarks at Edinburgh, describing Mr. Dadabhai Naoroji (who contested Holborn Division in 1886) as a "black man," that gentleman is about to address a public meeting in the same city at an early date. Lord Salisbury has a weakness for slighting references of this kind; he compared the Irish to Hottentots. But neither, reference, after all, carries so much with it as to describe a lie as— "a Salisbury."

And so the Warrington Corporation have decided to sell the vacant land in Bridge-street. The sum realised is not, perhaps, all that fancy painted it; but it seems it is as good as can be got. It is something to stop the loss of £9OO a year; for that is pretty near twopence in the pound. Of course, it wont do to be sanguine about having the rates reduced twopence next year because of this sale of land. The £9OO will simply be dropped in another hole--say, sewerage next time.

It is something to see the Warrington Town Council unanimous, as they were in supporting Councillor F, A. Roberts' motion for a return as to the number of Corporation Officials who have had "pickings" as "presiding officers and poll clerks at the recent municipal election in the borough." It is to be hoped the Council next month will be unanimous in saying to offenders—" Guitly, but, don't, do it again." It is very nice to be able to sell one's time "twice over,' and get good pay, too, but well,—it is not quite the thing; so "don't do it again."

A London Correspondent is responsible for the following bonnet story :—" The economists have discovered a rare piece of extravagance on the part of the Commander-in-Chief in the Mediterranean, which will be brought before Parliament. It appears that when the Duchess of Edinburgh went from Malta to Athens her bonnet-box was left behind. As soon as the mistake was discovered, a vessel of the Mediterranean squadron was ordered back to Malta for the missing box, and it was brought on to Athens at an expense of several hundred pounds to the British taxpayers."

It looks as if Lord Itat.dolph Churchill were setting about the task of forming another Fourth Party. He attacked the Government on Tuesday on their policy—or rather want of policy—in the Soudan, and had as his Conservative following Mr. Handbury, Mr. Jennings, Captain Heathcote, and Viscount Curzon. The Opposition voted with him, and he ran the Government a close race, but they just managed to win by a neck. It is an ill wind that blows nobody good, and, when Tory politicians fall out, there is a chance of the people getting their own.

1 Last Christmas, Warrington Union was disgraced through certain inmates of the Workhouse being made drunk by an over-supply of beer. It scorns it was Mr. Jolley vAio interfered to' ensure "pints each" when the Workhouse ;nester was supplying half-a-pint each. It is therefore a question how far the orgte was due to his mischievous meddling. There is to be a risk of another drunken scene ; a fewonly of the Guardians can profit by experience; beer is to be again supplied; pints each" to the men; half-pints to the women. We shall not blame the inmates, if some of them arc again locked up. • It is the majority of the Guardians, rather, who require to be put "under restrain." 11WW....0.0••.•

-- Lord Dufferin as V icertly seems to have turned tail in the matter of "reform" hi India. Last year he patted 'the natives on the back, and talked about, the possibility of their being "exten- sively associated with their English rulers in the administration of their own domestic affairs." To-day he expresses himself as being opposed to taking "a very big jump into the unknown by the application to India of democratic methods of government." He is afraid of Home Itule as applied to our great Dependency; but we are a long way off that. There is no fear of "a very big jump "—unless it be towards a mad war in search of "a scientific frontier." Lord Dufferin's progress is like Paddy's " advance " ; it is two steps backwards..

The Rector of Warrington had something to say the other week, on the virtue of Moderation; and it looks as if Mr. Clarke .Aspinall had been deliver- ing a reply in the Rector's presence. Anyhow, it. is a reply, for the distinguished Liverpool coroner, speaking at the Parish Church School, on Monday evening, said he was not at first an abstainer, but resolved to become one. "He felt that the aver- age working man would be more influenced by his talking to him as an abtainer than if he talked as the most moderate of non-abstainers. That was his experience, and it told him that in a little planting and watering of the seeds of temperance he had been able to do, he had been more success- ful to the outward eye, so far as he could gauge his work, than he had ever been, though he worked just as conscientiously before." Perhaps the Rector will ponder this saying, and go and do likewise.

DEFADUTIoN OF CKARACTER AT MMES.—Elizabeth Cook, a well-dressed married woman, of 27, Alforde-at., was summoned to Widnes Police Court, on Thursday., to antwer a charge of having used defamatory language towards Alice Shaw, a married woman who is caretaker of St. Paul's Mission Room. Mr. Knowles appeared for the complainant. It was alleged that on the 19th Novem- ber, the defendant accused the complainant of being a harlot, and made used of highly improper language. The Vicar came upon the scene, and attempted to act as peacemaker, but• his efforts were of no avail and the defendant called complainant filthy names in his presence. Several witnesses were called in support of the complaint and Mrs. Shaw was given a very good character.— The defendant acted in a very excited fashion and con- tended that the complainant was "nothing but a false swearer." She caused some amuse- meet by addressing Mr. Knocks personally, end alleged that he had told her that Mrs. Shaw was the worst woman in Widnes.—The Bench ordered the defendant to be bound over to keep the peace for six months, herself in £2O and two sureties of £lO each; or go to gaol forl4 days. The defendant declared that She would go. to gaol, and paid no heed to the entreaties of her husband. .She was conveyed to the cells with the prisoners, and her linsband and friends left the court. Sr. Luxes CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, MASON-STREET, RUNCORN.—The annual Sabbath School teachers meeting in connection with the above place, was held on Tues- day evening last. A most excellent tea was provided and partaken of, after which the business commenced, tho proceedings being presided over by the Rev. J. D. Thomas. After singing and prayer, the Secretary (Mr. Walterllacey) read the minutes of the previous meeting -which were confirmed. The Treasurer (Mr. Joseph Slade), presented his report for the past year which was unanimously adopted.. The election of officers was then proceeded with, resulting' in the .election of Messrs. J. J. Speakman (superintendent), W. Lacy (secretary), Joseph Slade (treasurer), and W. Hethering- ton (auditor.) Mr. J. J. Speakman, superintendent', then addressed the meeting, reviewing the past years work in which they had all taken part, planning out the Isst method to obtain success in the Sunday School. The funds of the school he was glad to say were in a flourishing condition, the' discipline of the 'school excellent. Mr. Speakman closed his remarks by giving a 'short sketch of his connection with the school for the last 25 years: Mr. Joseph Slade then made a short speech', as did Mr. George Lacy—who also sang a song. Mr. Walter Lacy gave a song. • The senior young.men's (Mr. Geerge Lacy's) class,—and the senior class, ladies' (Mrs. Powell's and Mrs. Lacy's class) were also present. The meeting was brought to a close with benediction by the Chairman.

DROWNING CASE Moortm.—On Tuesday a girl, twelve Years of age, daughter of Mr. Morris, farmer, Moss Side Farm, Moore, was drowned,under the following circumstances. The girl was nursing her brother, two years of age, and wandered away on the Marsh, which is rented lw Mr. Morris. Here she was surrounded by the tide of the Mersey, and in endeavouring to get to a place of safety she stumbled into a hollow in the land, and was drowned. The baby was kept afloat for some . moments by its clothing, and a Ship Canal laboerer succeeded in rescuing the infant, and conveyipg it home. Mr: Worsley. coroner, held an inquiry into the circumstances of the death at the Red Lion Inn, Moore, on Thursday. The father of the deceased, Thomas Morris, Moss Side, Norton, a farmer, said that on Tuesday deceased, with a sister two years of age, went to the Moss, and he afterwards heard that she had been drowned. Thomas Edwards, Moss Side, who is employed on the Ship Canal, deposed that at Ana noon on Tuesday he saw the deceased, with a child, on the Marsh. She was being sur- rounded by the rising tide, and was standing in a few inches of water. She had the child in her arms. Witness was 500 or GOO yards away at the time. He stopped an engine that he was in cherge of, and went to the aseislemee of the deceased, but before he reached her she was drowned. He saw the child being carried away by the tide, and rescued it. The water was very muddy. -After hearing the evidence, tlie jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased was drowned in the Mersey by being surrounded by the rising tide. LORD CROSS AT THE CARLTON CLUB.—=Visentint Cross, delivered a discourse at the City Carlteti Club on Tuesday night. He inquired h .Av it, came to pass that the Land Purchase Bill was opposed, and answered the question by stating that the order came from the great Triumvirate which, to the discredit of our system of government in Eng- land, was composed of a man who had been three times Prime Minister of England, Mr. Parnell. and* either- Jr. Dillon or Mr. Devitt." In order to throw a complete light on the present state of parties Lord Cross asides):—" Mr. , Gladstone could only ,take the line which was pointed not to him by Mr. Pernell. He had no power himself ;he was hound hand end foot.; he had sold himself, body and soul, to the Irish party, and Mr. Parnell was not on very Sound ground himvelf. Mr. Parnell knew that he had to bold Mr. Gladstone in hand if he possibly could; but he also knew that he had people behind him who wanted to go faster; and Mr. Parnell was just as much in the hands of Mr. Devitt and Mr. Bikgar as Mr. Gladstone was in the hands of Mr. 'Parnell. After such an explanation as this there is really nothing more to be said. Mr. Gladstone, it seems, can only take the line which is pointed out to him be Mr. Parnell. who in turn" has to hold Mr. Gladstone in hand if he possibly can "—a statement somewhat at variance with the original theory of Mr. Gladstone's helplessness ;whilst Mr. Parnell is himself completely in the power of Messrs. Devitt and Biggar. The Minister of India comforted his -hearers KM ewhat be informing them that in his opinion there would not be a general election for font years. Worsley, the Coroner, on Saturday held an inquest •at the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, on the body of Patrick Brennan, a labourer on the Ship Canal Works, who was found drowned in a lock on the Weston Canal, on ThUrsday night, under circumstances previously rprted. A verdict of "Accidentally drowned" was returned. The Coroner commented strongly on the necessity for a public highway from Runcorn direct to Weston Point. It was unfortunate that so many people -going to and from Weston Point and Runcorn should meet with their deaths on account of the bad road they had to tread. It was strange that there was no public highway where people could walk with safety, especially taking into consideration the habit that sailors had of getting drunk when they came from sea, and then to be turned out on this dangerous path, where they had little more than a yard or so to walk in some places along the canal. The greater number Of the inquests held there were owing to this, which he might say was a perfect death trap. It seemed impossible that a civilized people should allow this state of things tocontinue, when it might easily he obviated. It was not safe for a sober person to walk along, let alone one who was intoxicated, and in wet weather it was very bad, even in the daytime, as in some parts it was very slippery. The bottom lock gate would, in future, be left open, so that if any person wanted to get across the lock, they could walk across; the gate was guarded. This might tend to put a stop to one cause of the loss of these valuable lives. GALLANT CONDUCT OF A, BROTHER AT RUNCORN.—On Saturday afternoon, at Runcorn, Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, held an inquest on the body of Henry Moores, Ilatman, of 32, Okell-street.—Robert Moores. flat:flan, said the deceased was his brother, and was 24 years of age. On Thursday last they went in a small boat on the river Mersey, to the assistance of a man whose flat was on the sands near the Old Quay, where it had been driven. By some means the deceased fell into the water. It was dark, and no one saw him fall in, but as they were going round the Side of the fiat witness heard a plunge. He asked a boy on board what it was, and he replied " It is your brother in the river." Wit- ness saw the man in the water, and he jumped into about 12 feet of water to save him. He succeeded in getting hold of the end of the deceased's fingers ; but the tide running very strong bore the latter away from witness, who got on to the flat, and being told by the boy thst his brother was in the water at the other end of the flat, witness jumped into the water again. He swam round the ferry boats, but could not find his brother. The deceased could swim a little, but not very much. The accident happened about six o'clock in the evening. He supposed that in getting down the side of the flat, at the stern end, to get into the boat, about eight feet below, he stepped on to the gunwale of the boat, which tilted, and deceased was thrown into the water. There were plenty of people near, but as it was very dark they would not be able to see the man tumble ipto the river.—James Moores, another brother, a labourer, residing in Ashridge-street, said he dragged the river for the body on Friday morning, and recovered it.—The Coroner said he thought the jury would agree with him that Robert Moores had behaved in a most manly spirit, and had done the very best he could in deep water, with the tide running very strongly, to save his brother, but, nnfortunately.' his efforts were not successful. Robert Moores had acted as a brave and good man.—A verdict to the effect that the deceased was accidentally drowned was returned.

At the lliineorn Police Court, on Monday, Henry ,Williiims,, captain of the schooner Sarah Jane, was stirnnickned to answer a charge of having, on the 27th November, wilfully and corruptly given false evidence in his examination on oath, before his Honour Judge. Wynne Ffoalkes, judge of the Run- corn County. Court. on the hearing of an action in which John Blundell, lamilord of the Three Crowns Inn; King-st, was the plaintiff, and Williams the defendant. Mr. Wynne Humphreys appeared for the complainant and Mr. Shepherd Little, barrister (in- structed by Mr. • Barton), for the defendant —Mr. Huniphreyi.said he had seen Judge Ffoulkes. who was engaged on professional business that day, but would be able to attend Court on Monday next. Under these circumstances Mr. Humphreys applied for an adjourn- ment until that date.—Mr. Little said the defendant was a man of substance, cantain of a ship now ready to pro- ceed to sea. Neither ef the men, on whose behalf-Mr: Humphreys was preeeedinz in this case, were worth sixpence,or *suld be able toindemnify the clefendantfor costs. They had taken this action out of spite, simply for the purpose of preventing the defendant proceeding to sea, and it was for that object the adjournment was asked for. Mr. Little contended that Mr. Humphreys had taken the wmng course, and he argued that the case should he dismissed.—The magistrates said it was desirable that the defendant should proceed to sea, and: if Mr. Humphreys thought it was mate- rial that the county court judge should be present, they must dismiss the ease.—Mr. Humph- reys said it was very kind of his friend to refer to his motives, and the spite of his client. —Mr. Little: I said nothing about: my friend's motives at all.—Mr. Humphreys: I take allresnonsibility of seeing his honour and of bringing him into court, and the responsibility of applying for this adjournnient —Mr. Little said there was one responsibility his friend would not undertake— he would not indemnify the defendant in that action.for, if the defendant was proved innocent, he would have to take an action for dainages against two men who were worthless,as he could show.—Mr. Humphreys said if the bench were of opinion that the case should be dismissed he had not the remotest ohjection.—The case was dis- missed, and Mr. Little did not press an application for coats. Afterwards a fresh summons was taken out against Williams, and the case should be heard. on Monday.
SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN. TIIE CORONER'S INQUEST.

A shocking discovery was made at the works of the Buneorn Soap and Alkali Company on Tuesday morning. About half-past eight, -George Wild, a labourer, was passing an acid tower, when he kw a black looking object lying on the ground at the base, and-he was startled to find on examination that it was the dead and bruised body of Cliailes Simkin. The body was conveyed to the house of Simkins' parents on Mill Brow, and it this tran- spired that the deceased had not been hOme to his tea on the previous evening nor had he turned in during the night. On Monday Simkin was employed in tarring an' ncid tower about• 60 'feet high, and it was surmised from the position in which he was found that he hail fallen from the top; but as he was working alone. there were no witnesses of the accident. Mr. J. E. Worsley, the ooroner. on Thurf4day afternoon held an inquest on the body at the Bull's Head Inn. Mr. Hewett ; watched the proceedings on behilf of the firm, and

Inspector O'Donnell appeared for the police.— Robert Simkin, of Mill Brow, said the deceased was his I son, and was 28 years of age, lie had been employed for many years by Mr. T. Kirkham, and was accus- tomed to much more dangerous work than that he was engaged on at the Alkali Works. The deceased was not subject to giddiness or faittting.—William Dyer, foreman smith, who lived at the works, stated that the deceased asked him for a job on the 29th November, and he engaged him as a day labourer, and he set him to painting and tarring the acid towers. The deceased was accustomed to this kind of work. At the time of the accident the deceased would be tarring the large down pipe of the tower, and to do this he would stand on the wood frames that supported it. He did net know how the accident occurred. There was no chance of the deceased being overpowered by gas whilst he was on the work.—James Crank, of Lick-street, labourer, deposed that he saw the deceased at the foot of the tower about a quarter to four; he was then all right.— Levi Knowles, labourer, Trinity-street, said about four o'clock he was on the waste heap, about 100 yards from the tower' when he saw two pieces of timber and a I brush fallfrom the tower. Had the deceased fallen at the same time he must have seen him. He could not swear that the piece of wood produced was one that fell.—A juryman pointed out that the nails in the wood had quite rotted away.—The Coroner said he should like some explanation as to this piece of wood, and Mr. John Knowles, the works manager, gave evidence. He said the wood was a strut or stay, and had been fastened on one side to the timber, and on the other to the wooden carriage that took the pipes down. He did not suppose that any man would venture his life upon such a piece of weod. It had come from a place just below where the bucket of tar was.. The deceased could have stood upon that piece of wood to have tarred the outside of the pipe, but it was very improbable.—The Coroner said he had got it strongly into his mind that when that piece of wood fell the deceased also fell. Considering the state of the nails in that wood, if the jury had evidence that the man was standing upon it, and throueb it giving way he fell, he should think that was testimony of grave neglect, indeed, on the part of the owners of the works. They had no evidence of that kind, but the strut itself afforded sufficient evidence that the woodwork of the tower needed to be looked to In the works, the manager said he should have a railing put up at this place, and at the time he (the Coroner) considered the suggestion a very gad one, but he must say that unless the railing was better constructed than that strut appeared to have been, it would be a distinct source of danger. If protection was to be added, it must be of a very much more substantial character than that, and he hoped it would be seriously attended to.— Acting according to the directions of the Coroner, the jury returned a verdict of "Found dead.'?—The Comner said it appeared to him tha, nailing was not the proper way to put a stage together, and especially in a chem'eal works where iron was eaten away.—A juryman : But they never use any other way.—Mr. Hewett If the strut had been intended for a man to stand upon, it would have been strapped with knees.— Mr. Knowles said it was improbable that the deceased would stand upon the strut, because there would be a clear 80 feet of a drop below him, and he could do his work from the inside of the rail.—The Coroner said persons who were accustomed to scaffolding would trust a scantier thing than anyone else would do.—Mr. Hewett: That is the very reason why these accidents occur. Mr. Howett proinised that he would attend to the Coroner's observations.

div.head: STATISTICS.
div.p: STATISTICS.

The visitors reported that the returns for month end- ing 23rd November showed a total number on the rolls of 3,303: an average attendance of 2662.2; and a percent, age of attendance of 81. The above figures show on increase in the number on. the roll of 135, an increase in the average attendance of 252.5 and the percentage of attendances of 5, as compared with the corresponding period of last year. _ _

div.head: CENSUS OF_CHILDREN:INTRRESTING FIGURES.
div.p: CENSUS OF_CHILDREN:INTRRESTING FIGURES.

The Clerk read an elaborate report pf the educational census of the district. The enumeration had been done by two visitors, and had takm two days. We take the following figures from the report : • . Age. Boys. . Girls. Totals. Under 3 years 833 762 1595. 1595 Betw( en 3 and 5 507 497 1004 Sand 13 17°6 1705 3451 4'455 6050.

The number of clickiren attending sc-fiCrOl betivecn 3 and 13 years of age is 4,455—0 n the rolls of public ele- mentary schools 3,300, at private schools 300, leaving abientees to be accounted for 855. These absentees are for the most part children between 3 and 5 years ot age, who cannot be compelled to attend school. The report continues :—" It now remains to be seen whether the existing accommodation in the public elementary schools of Runcorn is sufficient for the numbers of children of school age, according to the rules of the edubational department. The total number between 3 and 13 years of age being 4,455, a deduction of 300 must be made for those attending private schools, leavlng4,lss. A further deduction of one-eighth, or 12.5 per cent., is allowed for absentees from reasonable causes, leaving 3,636, which is supposed to be the number of children for whom school seats should be found . Comparing this fig,urewith the existingcertified accommodation in Runcorn—viz 3,227 it would seem that we are 409 seats deficient, but when we compare it with the actual average attendance, viz., 2,626, it is at once seen that the departmental estimate of children is 1,000 greater than the reality. There is ample accommodation for the 2,626 whom we have, but not for 1,000 more who now make their appearance on paper."—The report was referred to committee for consideration.

div.head: BRAVE RUNCORN BOY.
div.p: A BRAVE RUNCORN BOY.

An interesting presentation to a boy named Gilbert Booth, was made at the conclusion of an inquest held at the Court Room, Runcorn, on Saturday afternoon. Th ere were "about 30 persona present. The facts of the affair are fully explained in the :,p-tteelt of the Coronet (Mr. J. E. Worsley), who made the presentation. The Coroner said they were there to do honont to a brave boy for saving another boy's life, and he himself had great pleasure in taking part in the .proceedings. Gilbert Booth.was 14 years of age, and was the son of John Booth. farmer, who lived at Bate's Bridge. He worked with his father on the farm.. Sornetime•age he was going along Halton- road, near to the .Bridgewater Canal, when ht. saw a little boy named William Shaw on the other side of the canal fall into the water. He thereupon, without any heSitation, left his horses in the road, got over the fence on to the canal side, dived into the water, and !Drought the. boy to land, and saved his life. (Applause.) The first intimatioa of the brave deed was discovered by the boy's father. It seemed that Wilbert Booth during the Jubilee festival in the summer of last year won a, watch., When he jumped into the canal he had the watch on• him, and some time afterwards his father -asked hint where it . was, and was told that he had taketbit to be repaired. His . father remonstrated with him al;sett his not taking care of the watch, and Gilbert told him he had been in the canal 'kith it. and that was .the first intimation the father had of his son saving William Shaw's life. Gilbert 800 II did not seem to think that he had done anything great, otherwise he weuld have mentioned the. act, and ,his • modesty was as com- mendable as the act of 'bravery he displayed. Some people, however, did not thinks the act should be passed over in that way, and amongst them was Mr. croley— (applause)—andMr. Croley took the matter up,iand the result had been that the Royal Humane Society had acknowledged the brave act. Before ,this was done, however, he (the Coroner) wrote to Superintendent Hollingworth, who instructed the Inspector to make inquirip, and the circumstances of the case were fully cerroborated, and it was found that the boy had undoubtedly saved the . child's lire. Thereupon the report was sent to the Royal Humane Society, and the boy Booth was awarded their testimonial, which was under the signature of the President, the Duke of Argyll. (Applause.) Ile was sure that all present would say of Gilbert Booth that he was a credit to his parents, that he was a credit to his town, and that he was a credit to his countrymen--(applause)---and they would ,all wish that the course which he had commenced in his 'early life would be continued, and that aS hs grew up he would prove to be as brave a* man as be had proved him, self to be as a lad. (Applause.) Ire (the. Corner) had hoped to have had present Mr. Chadwick, J.:P., who, however, had been unable to come; but Mr. t hadwick hail asked him in his name to -give Booth a sovereign: (Applause.) Mr. W. Shaw (rnissionaryi then; read the address, which was en yellt,m, and made a few appropri, ate remarks. Mr. Lt Tbvenherg moved. Mr. S. Yarweecl seconded, and Mr. Croley supported, a vote of thanks to the Coroner, which was unanimously accorded. Mr. Croley remarked that the Comer had presented Booth with a coat and a cap.
