div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

A monthly meeting of this Tow,' Council was held in the Council Chamber, Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Sutton) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Holmes, Harrison, Davies, Burgess, Webster; Councillors Platt, Tinsley, Shaw Green, Ashton, 4 Voisey, Flood, Heaton, Black h urst, Jenkins, Percival, J Taylor, H. Roberts, Wright, Monks, Fleming. Jolley, Greenall, F. A. Roberts, Hutchin- son, J. Pierpoint, Francomb ; Messrs. Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor), Dr. Gornall (medical officer), and Chorley (borough treasurer). WATCH COMMITTER. This Committee had resolved that Alderman Harrison be appointed the deputy-chairman of the Committee. It was also resolved roat Councillor Francomb and Coun- cillor Jolley be appointed the Visiting Committee of Vie Bridewell. On the motion of the Mavoit, seconded by Councillor Joluarr, the minutes were confirmed. FINANCE COMMITTER. . .

This Committee's minutes recorded the appointment of Alderman Holmes as chairman, and Councillor Green- ing, as deputy-chairman. On the motion of Alderman HOLMES, seconded by Councillor SHAW aax, the minutes were confirmed. STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COM- MITTEE.—SALE OF THE BRIDGE-ST. LAND. Resolutions: "That Councillor Platt be appointed Chairman. and Councillor Greening the deputy Chair- man of this Committee for the ensuing year ; 'that the following members of tee Committee be appointed the Lighting sub-Committee :—Councillors Greening (con- vener), Platt, H. Roberts, Blackhurst, and Wright ' • that the following members be appointed a visiting Com- mittee to visit the sites of proposed buildings, or alterations to buildings, when required ;—Councillors Platt, Greening, Wright, Marsh, H. Roberts. The Lighting sub-Committee recommended various altera- tions to old lamps, and also the erection of several new lamps. CouncillOr Ptarr moved the confirmation of the minutes. He thought the Council should be as fully informed as possible as to the state of the negotiations with respect to the proposed new street from Bridge-st.; to Wilson-Patten-st. Since the last meeting of the Council the Committee had had a communication from the London and North-Western Railway Company, which stated that the Company still adbered to their offer to the Corporation of December, 1884, upon the further condition that the right of public way from Wilson-Patten-st past Arpley S ation be extinguished on the opening of the new street. The Committee, Mr. Platt said, could not aeries to this. They were not prepared to give up the right of way past Arpley Station even in order to get such an advantage as the new street would be. (Hear. hear) There was one matter that had slipped out of the Council summons—that with regard to the sale of land in Bridge-street. The resolution passed by the Committee was "That the offer of Mr. T. E. Wright for the purchase of the whole of the surplus land between Friars'-gate and the buildings now in course of erection, at £2 10s. per yard, be accepted." He might say that the form in which the resolution appeared was scarcely accurate, because it simply included front land, and not back land. The price might, perhaps be looked upon as being rather low—(hear, hear)—and the Street Improvement Committee would have been exceedingly glad if they could have got more money for the land, and they would still be glad if a reasonable way for getting more money for the land could be shown. (Hear, hear.) That On the minutes was the best offer they had; in fact, he might say, the only definite offer they had had SinCe the first lots were sold. In August of the present year the Committee succeeded in selling two lot at £2 10e. per square yard. The other lets, higher up the street, had always been supposed to be rather more valuable, and perhaps that was so; but on this occasion they received an offer for the whole of the plot, and that being so, the Committee were perhaps rather easier to deal with than they would otherwise have been. If any member of the Council could show tat a higher price cOuld be obtained, or that any greatsT advantage could he gained by throw- ing over the present bargain, the Committee would be glad to take that course, only they would be very sorry to lose a definite offer which would CliqDoSe of a large portion of the land The quantity of land offered for sale was about 1,336 square yards, and at the price offered the amount realized would be £3,350. He had reason to believe that if the ground were sold to the present applicant substantial shops would almost immed:ately be erected. Councillor BLACICHERST seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor Watene said that as his name had been mentioned, he wished the Council to understand that he was not making that offer for himself, but simply for a Hear, hear.) Councillor FLRMINO objected to the sale of the land at the figure named. He believed that the first portion of the land was sold at £5 per yard, the second at £5, the next at £3 10s., the next at £3 10s., and then the land on which the Roebuck stood, which was sold at equal to £4. The next lots were sold at £2 12s. ed. Committer PLATT said that if Councillor Fleming would refer to his Council minutes he would find that £2 10s. was the price. Councillor FLAMING said he would take it as £2 lOs was of opinion that the plot at the corner was worth about £5. He moved as an amendment that the matter be referred back to the Committee for further consider- tion . (Hear, hear.) Councillor JOITN PIRRPOINT said he felt very strongly upon that subject. The Town Clerk would bear him eut when he said that he asked on behalf of some clients, whether £3 per yard would be accepted if the purchasers took the entire lots which were then unsold, from the bottom of Bridge-street up to Friars'-green end. This was about 24 years ago and he was then told by the Town Clerk that the Committee would not take less. than something like £4. There was no doubt that with the Ship Canal and other improvements they could see before them the land would very shortly be taken, and his impression was that, to speak within range, they would realize at least £3 or 1,3 10s. per yard for it. The MAYOR remarked that in discussing that question they ought not to overlook the fact that they had already been in possession of the land for five years, without scarcely a bid having been made for it. They should also recollect that £2 10s. was now equal to about £3 2s. 6d. in four years' time. (" No, no.") Well, that was his calculation. Alderman Dimes suggested that the matter be referred back to the Committee for one month which weuld give time for other offers, if any, to be made. (Hoar, hear.) The MAYOR: I should like to know from Mr. Wright whether that offer would be accepted. Councillor Wmowr said he liked the suggestion very much. They wanted everything done straiehtforwardly arid openly. He must however consult his client. Councillor JOLLEY considered that it was to the interest of the Corporation to see the land covered with buildings as early as possible, and he should support the ~Coinrnithee in selling the land at £2 10s., because that WAS the highest offer they could get. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Botroe agreed with Alderman Davies's ,suggestion. He expressed snrprise that no account was :given of the back land, and no mention made of the price at which that would be sold if the front land was Geld at £2 lbs. At this point Councillor WRIGHT riq't the Council Chamber in order to consult his client as to the proposed deferment of the minute. Councillor MONKS believed that the price now offered for the land was as good a price as they could get any man with his head on his shoulders to givethem. (Hoar, hear.) Councillor VOISRY objected to a month being fixed. He was rather in favour of, and should support, Coun- cillor Fleming's amendment, that no stated time be fixed, but that the matter be left over. The price at present offered did not, in his opinion, represent the capital value of the land., Couneillor FRANCOMB mentioned that he knew a gentleman who had said he was prepared to give a much bigger sum for the land than that offered by Councillor Wright. He thought if the land was put up to auction again better offers would be received. The MAYOR said it seemed rather strange that some- body should came forward now and say that they were prepared to give so much. If they could defer the matter for a month he thought that would be the best course. - - -

Councillor 11. ROBERTS said he did not think the defer- ment of the question for a month would meet the difficulty at all. They would not get any considerable advance within the next four weeks. They might have some people making a step above Councillor Wright to the extent of Is. or 25., but he considered that it would be unfair to allow that sort of thing to take place. (Hear. hear.) That offer of Councillor Wright's ought to be either on or off that night. If, however,. the Coun- cil thought the question should be deferred he should be in favour of its postponement, not for four weeks, but for five or six months. (Hear, hear,) Councillor WRIGHT, on returning to the Council Chamber, intimated that his client desired him to say that he washy no means eager about the purchase. If the Council declined the offer that night the matter was at an end so far as he was concerned. Ccuncillor TINSLEY said that he felt certain that another client would appear if the matter was allowed te stand over. Alderman Buttonss said that he could not help coming to the conclusion that it was the duty of the Council to support the Committee in what they had done with reference to the sale of the land in Bridge-st. If the person Mr. Wright had been to see had consented to allow the matter to remain open he should have been very glad, but he could not lose sight of the fact that the Corporation had had this land on their hands too long, and it had been much too costly. He did not think that much would be gained by waiting for an improved offer. If the land was built upon they would have the rating of the property. Councillor J. SHAW-GREEN said that ever since the land was offered for sale it had been going down in value. Although gentlemen had said that they thought there were gentlemen in the town who would pay more money, there bad been no definite pledge made. He should vote .• for the passing of the minutes of the Committee.
Councillor rIiRCITAL also supported the minutes, and Alderman atvias remarked that what he had said

before was only a suggestion. He should now vote for the passing of the minutes. The amendment was then put to the meeting with the following result :—For the amendment: Councillors John Pierpoiat, Fleming, Francornb, Heaton. Voisey, Tinsley, and Ashton (7) ; against Aldermen Holmes, Burgess, Davies. Webster, and Harrison, and Councillors Platt. Crreenall, Monks, Jolley, Illackhurst, J. Shaw Green, Hutchinson, Percival, J. Taylor, H. Roberts and the Mayor (16). The amendment was therefore lost. Councillor Ftemine asked why bay windows had been erected in Bridge-st. He considered that they were a hideous sight. Councillor BovroN : Is the Bridge-st. land to be built upon? Councillor Witioirr : Before very long, I believe. you will find the whole street covered with substantial build- ings. Councillor PLATT observed that he did not think Councillor Wright would agree with Councillor Fleming as to the very ornate ereetions he (Mr. Wright) had been put ing up being hideous. The Committee would treat every case on its merits. ' If a proposed bay window appeared to be an obstruction to the street it would not be allowed, but if it would form an improvement to the general character of a building it would be foolish to oppose it. The minutes were then adopted.
SANITARY COMMITTEE AND THE INTERCEPTING
DEPOTS.

This Committee's minutee contained tile following resolutions :—That Mr. Alderman Burgess be appointed Chairman, and Mr. Alderman Sutton (Mayor) the Deputy-Chairman, of this Committee for the ensuing year: that Councillors Francomb (conv:ner), Wright, and H. Roberts be appointed a Sub-Committee to superin- tend the horses, vans, stables, and provender, and all matters pertaining thereto, and to report to the Com- mittee: that the Chairman, Deputy-Chairman, and Councillors Greening, H. Roberts, Wright, and Voisey, be appointed a Sub-Committee to visit the Longford and Intercepting Dept,ts, and to report to the Committee; that the Chairman, Deputy-Chairman, and Councillors Francomb and Voisey be appointed a sub-Committee to visit the Infectious Diseases Hospital, and to report to the Committee; that a con-ract be entered into with Mr. W. Sharratt, of Manchester, for the purchase of catholic powder required by the Corporation during three years commencing Ist November instant. at £8 per ton : that any frOsh arrangements with regard to the management of Longford works be deferred for three months, and that Owen Warner, the engineer, be paid 103. per week in addition to his ordinary wages for his extra duties. Alderman BCRAIEIRS, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said Mr. Warner had given considerable satis- faction to the Committee, and it was felt that he had a claim upon them. At the same time, while his work had been done satisfactorily, the Committee felt they would rather have time—three months—before they came to any decision with reference to the management of he Longford works. Councillor FatIICOMB seconded.

CAURCiIIOr FLAMING: What salary has Warner? Alderman BURGESS: 375. a week as engineer, and the house we built there te live in ; but it is understood that he lives in the house as caretaker, so that we may have someone on the premises during the night. Alderman DATIBS : I think he deserves to live rent free at Longford. (Laughter.) Councillor Ptarr said he had again to call the attention of the Sanitary Committee to the state of things exist- ing at the Intercepting Depots. The members of the Council had had promises without number that the matter would be attended to, and it was long ago since a Promise wa; made that a definite iac_miry aheidd be' held. The first thing to consider was whether there was a nuisance or not, but even that seemed to be a disputed point by same members of the Committee. He did not know how many. At any rate, some were not even prepared to admit that there was a nuisance, and until they were it was hopeless to think they would set about finding a remedy. ; (Hear, hear.) The people in the neightrmrhood of the Intercepting Depot, however, were fully per- sualed that a nuisance existed: they " had had painful experience that it was so. (Hear, hear.) He VMS in possession of a statement which had been signed by 1,000 persons, householders in the neighbourhood and it was as follows:—"W, the undersigned, testify to the fact that the working of the Intercepting Depot in Hardy- street causes a disgusting and offensive nuisance, which in the interest of the health of the inhabitants ought to be at once suppressed." (Hear, hear.) That had been signed by the householders, and every signature was well authenticated, and he considered thrtt a statement of that kind ought to carry conviction to the minds of the Committee that there was a nuisance. It was now more than two years since the depOt was established, and he did no, think it was in a better state now than when it was started, and the sooner the matter was taken in hand the better it would be for the health of the inhabitants. (Hear, hear.) They had already been told by the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee that that above all other Committees had no right to cause a nuisance in the borough, and in that remark every member of the Council would agree; the only thing was hat when the Committee had made up their minds to that effect they ought to set about remedying the nuisance and not leave it unabated for years. (Hear, hear.) What he had read was not a memorial, but a statement of fact by persons living in the neighbourhood. He should be happy to show it to the Committee, not to hand it over entirely to them, but for them to form an opinion about it. Councillor JANKINS said that as one of the represen- . _ _

tatives of INThrth-ast Ward he thought it was his duty to make careful inquiry about the mater which Councillor Platt had brought under the -notice of the Council He found that those living in the neighbourhood of the depot were almost universally of opinion that they had grounds of complaint. He had made a personal inspection of the:depot, and tested the matter on various occasions —when there was no wind and when there was a wind— and he could personally testify to the fact that when there was a south-west wind, and sometimes when a south-east wind, the effluvia from the depot was such that he should not like to reside near it. (Hear, hear.) As long as he had the pleasure of a seat in the Council Chamber he intended to raise his voice on behalf of the poorer residents of the ward which he, represented. (Hear, hear.)_

, Councillor Fr.nsmra also protested against the nuisance caused by the depot, which was in his opinion one of the greatest possible nuisances. If any member of the Council lived in the neighbourhood he would very soon do something to remove the nuisance. Councillor BOLTON said that as a representative of a ward in which one of the intercepting depots was situated, he was pleased to be able to state that the Committee were beginning to take steps in the right direction. as they were about to try a series of experi- ments with the intention of getting rid of the stench. (Hear, hear.) He hoped they would be successful. He was told also that when the vans were worn out it was intended to get a fresh class, and that they would be of such a character that the smell would not be able to escape. (Hear, hear.) ..

Councillor HEATON said that having gone thoroughly into the matter he had no doubt that a nuisance existed, , though he believed it was principally owing to negli- gence. He did not think sufficient care was taken. The stench at times was sufficient to make one put his handkerchief to his mouth and turn up another street. Councillor PERCIVAL endorsed the complaints as to a nuisance, and thought it would have been much better ' if the nuisance bad been confined to Longford. Alderman BURGESS had listened to the various remarks which had been made with reference to the interceptinr depots, and he could assure the Members of the Council that it was a great relief to him, and no doubt to the Mayor as deputy-chairman of the Committee, to find that nothing had been said about Longford DepOt. (Laughter.) The whole battery now had turned upon • the intercepting depots. Well, wheelie bad to say that night he would say as the lawyers did hat "this is without prejudice." (Laughter.) He had to remind Councillor Platt that he had no recollection of promises having been made, or of promises given not having been carried out. He had no knowledge of anything of that kind, for he had distinctly and determinedly set his face against making an admission of any kind. He would tell the Council why. Whatever he might say in the Town Council, or anywhere else, with reference to the intercepting deprits—if he admitted theywere a nuisance —it would be recorded against him and against the Council, and the matter would probably come up in a court of law some elay as evidence he had furnished, and he could not afford to do that. He had said often, and he repeated it that night, that of all the people in Warrington or elsewhere, a sanitary authority was the last body that should create a nuisance; and if it was shown that a nuisance existed, it was their bounden duty to set themselves to work to abate that nuisance and to abolish it. (Hear, hear.) The Council knew the difficulties the Committee had had; they had not had a shilling they could lay out to try even an experiment. They were told they must abate the nuisance, but that they must not have the money to enable them to do so. (Laughter.) Councillor Bolton had told the Council something which was quite true, namely, that before they saw or heard of the memorial to which reference. had been made that evening, the Borough Surveyor had made a suggestion to the Committee that he would like to be allowed to try an experiment which he believed would be successful and remove any cause of complaint. They had authorized him to do so, but they had to borrow in every direction the plant required. Some had lent one thing and some another. The Committee dare not ask the Town Council for money. (Laughter.) The consequence was that an experiment would be made in the course of three or four days, and Councillor Percival would be relieved of all anxiety about his ward. If the experiment was successful, and the Borough Surveyor believed it would be, it would cost a small sum, and lead to a permanent abatement of the nuis- ance, if Caere was one. The MAYOR thought what was required was patience. He was quite satisfied the Committee were determined to do all they could to abate any nuisance which might exist. They only wanted to be perfectly satisfied that a nuisance did exist, and in the second place to know how to deal with it to remove the cause of complaint altogether. The minutes were then agreed to.

Alderman flawless agreed that the cube setts were to be purchased at a low price, and he hoped that they were of a good and sound character, and would stand the work required of them. With regard to the recom- mendation that a width sufficient for a cart road be re-laid with setts opposite the works of Messrs. Itylands, he should like to know whether that width was in the centre of the street, or en the north side of it, and whether the putting down of another portion in mace; darn was for the purposed of making a less noisy road- way near to the Parish Church. If that was so, he thought it was a desirable thing to do. Councillor H. 'ionisers, referring to the price of setts, said that he knew that the Corporation would not be able to buy them at 14s. 6d. per ton for many weeks longer, and it would be desirable to purchase as many now as they could afford to do. Alderman Davies, replying, to Alderman Burmass, said that the part of the street referred to was on what Alder- man Burgess would call the North side, although he (Alderman Davies) thought that, strictly speaking, it inclined to the West. With regard to the purchase of setts they would talk to the surveyor. The report of the Committee was then approved. _ SCHOOL ATYPINDA.NCH COMMITTNH. _

Councillor Fiancomn propo4ed the confirmation of the minutes, and, the motion haying- been seconded by Councillor J. TAYLOR, was carried. GENERAL PURPOSES commrrrEE.—COUNTY COUNCILLORS &c.

The minutes of this Committee contained the ing recommendations :—(1) That the Mayorbe appointed chairman, and Mr. Alderman Pickmere deputy-chair- man, of the Committee for the ensuing year. (2) That the following members he appointed a sub-committee to act as a Parliamentary Committee r--.-,The Mayor (convener), Aldermen Burgess, Davies, Holmes, Pick- mere, Chandlev, Webster, and Councillor Greening. (3) That the following members be appointed a sub- committee to report as to the most appropriate places to be secured by the Corporation for the purposq of forming open spaces and recreation grounds in the borough :—Alderinerr Holmes (convener), the Mayor, Aldermen Crosfield, Davies, and Councillor Platt. The Town-Clerk reported to the Committee- that he had received the, writ for the election of three County Councillors for the borough, and it was resorved that the names of the following gentlemen be submitted to the Council for selection as suitable candidatmto represent the Borough on the County Council :—A/dbrriran Davies, Mr. John Fairclough, Alderman Crosfleld, Cbuncillor F. A. Roberts, and Councillor Monks. The Committee also recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £260 14s. 7d., including £l3B is. ed. election expenses . The Mayon proposed the confirmation, of the minutes, and Alderman DAviouseconded the proposition. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS, as an amendment, proposed that the recommendation that accounts amounting to L'2Bo 14s. 7d., incibding £l3B is. ati. for election expenses, be referred back to the Committee, to await the result of a motion of which he had given notice. Councillor Bomos.thought that the Cbuncil shoAd go , into Committee wheu considering the question of County . Council candidates. He should like tohave more infor- ; mation than he at present had. He did not believe in ,two or three men, or a Committo4 thinking for the whole town, without giving a reason. He also thought that three geotlemen and not five should have been mentioned. With regard to the amendinent he was of opinion that if councillor F. A. Roberts thought that the officials had been twice paid ho was entitled to what he asked for. Councillor Moults said that with regard to the County Council minute, he for one should withdraw his narae from the list. When he was spoken to about the matter there was certainly no intention of having one's name submitted to be canvassed as to whethbr one was a fit and proper person, and all the rest of it, and he was not going to put himself in a position in which he was going to oppose, or seem to oppose, any other gentlemen. He was not at all anxious for the position, which was one that would entail a great deal of time, trouble, and expense. Any gentleman who undertook the duties would find, he was sure, that in a money point of view it would cost at least £5O a year. ' Ho thought that the Committee should have selected three names only. He should withdraw his name because he was not anxious to appear to be in opposition to anyone else. Councillor H. ROBERTS, Said that personally he •, approved of the motion that Councillor F. A. Roberts had given notice of, so that the question of employment of Corporation officials as presiding officers and poll clerks

MR. BRIGHT'S Itrrutss.—Mr. Bright passed a better night en Wednesday, but Dr. llayle reported that his patient was weaker on Thursday morning. At one o'clock on Thursday, Mr. Bright was calm and quite. On Thursday the body of Hugh Cunningham, who had been atiending a fair at Rathfrilland, in county Down, was found on the road about a mile from the village. It is believed that he has been murdered, and four arrests have been made.

Tux SWEATING SYsram.—The Select Committee inquir- ing into the sweating systan sat again on Thursday morning, under the presidency of Lord Dunraven. Mr. Arnold AVhite, who has already given evidence relative to Government work, was re-called. He stated that the women who did the work were ignorant of the rate of pay settled by the Admiralty, and were, therefore, cheated out of a portion of their wages. might be put upon a satisfactory basis. The account, however, was not a large one, considering that nearly the whole of the borough was polled. He believed that the customary fee was three guineas for a presiding officer, and one guinea for a poll-clerk, and he did not quite see that they could go behind that arrangement. The Town Clerk must in these matters have a certain amount of discretion, which he was not inclined to cur- tail. He found a difficulty in supporting the amend- ment, because he did not see how in fairness they could expect fees that had been paid to be returned. Alderman 8J11101499 said that since he received the notice paper it had come to his knowledge that one of the officials in his department had had such an appointment as Mr. F. A. Roberts' motion referred to. So far as he knew, while the official in question had duties to perform which should not be neglected under any conditions— one was to be in his office to , receive complaints from ratepayers as to any nuisance that might arise—no one connected with the Committee was consulted by that official when he allowed himself to be appointed. He thought there was a want of discipline there that should not be allowed. He thought, however, that Mr. F. A. Roberts had sufficiently got the opinion of the Council, and would ask him not to press the amendment. If it occurred again he should be prepared to support Mr. Robert&

Councillor JeNLINS said that the Town Clerk was bound, on the occassion of an election, to have a staff of men who were perfectly competent to conduct an election under the Ballot Act. He knew from experience how difficult it was to get men who had been accustomed to the duties to be performed, aid he was inclined to think that if the Town ulerk had not discretion in this matter they might be put to a considerable expense in some other way, by an election being conducted loosely, or some action being taken in consequence of the inefficiency or carelessness of some official who had not performed his work in a satisfactory manner. At the same time, he thought that every employee of the Council should get the consent of his Committee before acting._

The TOWN CLBRE said that he did not think the matter in any way reflected upon him. None of the money went into his pocket. It had been the practise to employ officialsof the Corporation, who had gained An experience which made their services very valuable. He had never inquired if the officials had got per- mission to act. The matter should be settled in future by the General Purposes Committee. Councillor F. A. RORNRTS at this point intimated that he would withdraw the amendment to the minutes of the Committee, but not the motion that stood in his name.

Councillor PLATT said he thought Corporation officials should not be employed in any duties where they might even be supposed to know in which direction the 'voting was going, for in many cases it might be a matter of serious moment to them. He did not blame the Town Clerk at all ; he had taken the customary course. He thought that men in the town could be found to do the duties and it would be very much better if Corperation officials were not employed at all. Councillor BOLTON thought that the General Pur- poses Committee should give some explanation why they had selected County Council candidates at all. The question of representation on the County Council was one of vital importance to Warrington. Alderman DAVIES said that, as regarded himself, he had no time to attend to the duties of the office. He thought they should have younger men, who could give time and hard work.

The Maron said that someone must take the initiative in these matters. The reason why the General Purposes Committee took the matter up was because a notice was sent to him, signed by four gentlemen connected with the town, sumsting that the names they mentioned should be selected, the desire being to avoid an election. The desire of the Committee was simply to name the men they thought most competent. Alderman Dolmas said that as Alderman Davies and Councillor Monks would not fiat in with the recom- mendation, he did not see how they could confirm the minutes at all.

Councillor VOISHY thought that the General Purposes Com Matte should hare been content with submitting three names and not five. Councillor H. ROBERTS said that this matter was of so much importance to Warrington that they scarcely realized the value of it. There was the important ques- tion of the extension of the borough boundary, that had been referred to the consideration of the County Coun- cil for settlement. Now was the time to send men to the Council who would go in fer haying the boundary extended. He thought that it was ef the utmost impertance that the Council should meet specially to consider the question. In his *pinion Alderman Davies and Councillor Monks would be two of the most suitable men, and he thought Councillor F. A. Roberts would be a suitable man.

COll=lllol' MONIES said he had always thought that th e municipal boundary should be co-terminous with the Parliamentary boundary. If the borough was so ex- tended it would bring the population up to 50,000, and Warrington would then be in the category of boroughs entitled to be counties in themselves.

The Tows CLERK : 11 would give you over 50,000, and then application would have to be made to the Local Government Board, if that was thought desirable. Tie MAYOR We want limn to help us to get the borough made into a county. Ultimately it was resolved that the minutes of the Committee be passed, with the exception of that portion referring to County Council candidates, in regard to which it was decided that a special meeting should be held.
COUNCILLOR F. A. ROBERTS. MOTION.

Councillor F. A. Itommrs moved "That a return be given at the next monthly meeting of the Council of the namesof the presiding officers and poll clerks at the recent municipal elections in the borough. In case any Corporation employes have done these duties, that the amount of their salary be named, as well as the special fee for the occasion, together with the maximum fee allowed under the Act ; also for a return as to whether these officials, if any, had previously received the per- missionof the Committees under which their ordinary duties are performed for such special employment, and allowed to accept the fee for such services." The motion was agreed to unanimously, but the dis- cussion of the matter was deferred till the next meeting, when the return asked for will be furnished. The Committee then rose.

RUNCORN TRIM BLURS T. RUNCORN PARISH CHUH.CH.— A match between the aboTe teams vra,s played on the Blues' ground on Saturday afternoon. A good game resulted. True Blues 2 goals and 6 minors to Parish Church, 1 goal, 1 try, and 1 miner.

, WESTON IST V. ROYAL OAR WANDRIIIIES.—This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday, and after a splendid game victory rested with the home team by 1 goal, 8 tries, 4 minors, to one minor, Pendle- bury gaining 6 tries, Whitby 2, and Banks 1. Sr. HRLIINS BEIIWBRY Y. WILDRIISPOOL BDENVEIZY.— These teams composed of employes of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., had an encounter on Saturday which was of an even character, the result being a draw, the score being—St. Helens, one try and four minors; Wilderspool, one try and three minors. WIDNRS HALTON View V. DITTO& RRCEEATION IST. A match came off between thesh two clubs at Ditton on Saturday. Ditton had decidedly the best of the game all through, and came out winners by 2 tries, 5 minors, to nil. P. Wright and Fazackerly got the tries Tanner played well for the View, while Rawlinson, Whitefield, and Gilbody did very fairly for Ditton. WYCLIFER V. HALTON.—This match was played On the ground of the former on Saturday. The home captain lost the toss, and Jones kicked off. No return was made, and a scrimmage was formed in the visitors' quarters. Wycliffe pressed for a time, until a good kick by the Halton full heck sent the oval in touch at half way. Not r to be denied, the home team gradually worked the ball up the field, and Jones, getting hold, made a dashing run in. Williams took the place, but failed to improve. This roused the Halton men, and they began to press, a long kick by a full back scoring a dead ball. Jones dropped ow, and good following up on the part of the Wycliffe forwards prevented a return being made. Good play by Emmerson and Brundrett resulted in a minor being conceded, and half-time was called with the score —Wycliffe, 0-1-2; Halton, 0-0-2. After the restart Scott was conspicuous with a good run and kick, and the fovrards getting up well, Sumners got a try, but, on appeal, this was disallowed. Wycliffe continued to press, and Jones raced round his opponents and got over the line, but lost the ball, Clayton completing the try, but this was also disallowed. A scrimmage was formed close to the line, and Brundrett, passed nicely to Scott, who ran in at the corner-flag, Sampson failing at goal. Time was now called, leaving Wycliffe winners by 0-2-2 to Halton, 0-0-3 Sampson was in good form at full back for the home team, as were also Brundrett, Emmerson, and Scott. RUNCORN "A" TRAM Y. RUNCORN RECREATION.—TheSe teams met on the Irwell-lane ground, Runcorn, on Satur- day, and a great amount of interest was occasioned, there being a large number of spectators present. The ball was put into play by the Recs., but Davies returned and carried the sphere to the latter's quarters. Here a series of scrimmages took place. Cawley relieved for a time, and play was confined to the centre of the field. A neat Mt of play was afterwards executed by Evans, and the Recs. ground was a scene of hostilities. The ball was taken possessisn of by Stubbs, Shaw, and Bowyer, and Witblade was under the necessity to save. Booth returned, when the Runcorn forwards, who were led by ' Stubbs, Shaw, Barker, and Bowyer, compelled play to be I ccnfined again to their epponente quarters, Houghton, I however, came to the rescne, and by a grand kick clearedl the way for his side. Crompton made a splendid run, and peeled to Davies, who put in one of his neat runs, . and was within an ace of scoring. The Recreation team were afterwards compelled te save; but shortly after the drop-out Davies, Kearsley, and Stubbs showed a com- mendable piece of play for the Recreation. A grand run was later en put in by Booth, and the Recreation were forced back to the line, were Crompton obtained a mag- nificent try. Some disappointment was felt at the failure of Booth to convert a try into a goal. The score at half-time was—Runcorn: 1 try 3 minors; Recreation, nil. In the second half the play was of a similar charac- ter, being very fast and exciting, and at the close of the game the register was—Runcorn, 1 try 8 minors ; Recrea- tion, 1 minor. Teams :—Runcorn : S. Booth, back; T. H. Davies, J. H. Crompton, and W. H. Cawley, three- quarter backs ; W. Evans, and J. Hollingevorth, half backs; J. Gatley (captain), W. Shaw, W. Bowyer, W. Stubbe, J. Dutton, E. Lunt, H. Barker, W. Rigby, and G. Tipper, forwards. Recreation: W. Wislade, back ; Burton, Houghton, and T. Robinson, three-quarter backs; J. Cawley, J. Jones, half backs; R. Lowe, F. Acton, J. Acton, J. Kearsley, W. Moores, J. Jones, J. Davies, J. Stubbs, and D. Speakman, forwards. WIDNES T. ROCHDALTI Sr. CLRMEINT'S (IST TRAMS).— A very pleasant match was played en the Widnes ground on Saturday, when the Rochdale St. Clement's visited the chemical town for the first time this season. The result of the game was not very satisfactory as far as the visitors' ideas were concerned, although some good play on both sides was witnessed by nearly 3,000 spectators ; but the home team came out decidedly the best in the score. The passing tactics of the St. Clement's was worth attention, Out their opponents. with their well- known white suit seemed heavier looking than those of the faded blue guernseys, and as a matter of fact could " twist " them in the pack. In consequence of the recent rains the ground was rather slippery, but this did not tend to interfere much with the game. Widnes won the toss, and elected to play down the slope, and at once displayed their superiority, two minors being added for a start. The visitors welled to the home territory, and Thompson had a near escape in dropping a goal for Rochdale. Play was taken back by the Widnes defence, followed shortly afterwards by Farrell gaining the first try, amid Some applause, and Plumpton was successful in converting it into the major poiat. The Clement's fortress was again invaded, but the sphere was returned, after which a free kick by Parkinson once more converted matters to the " guernsey's " end, and for some time the goal was in danger, but relief was granted ia the shape of a pack in the centre. Farrell followed up the ball as it was going into the visitors' 25, but the Saints were Obliged to kick dead, after which half-time was called, with the score—Widnes, one goal ' four miners; St. Clement's, one minor. On the change of ends, Farrell kicked off, followed up by the home forwards, and in a short time Shepherd returned. His career being stopped, a line out followed. The oval then went the round of the field, settling in the Saint's territory, and being followed up by Kiddie and others, I that player eventually succeeded in rushing the belle over the line, and another try was registered, which Plumpton improved. Play continued in .the visitors quarters, several free kicks and scrimmages taking place in quick succession. The visitors' now assumed the aggressive, and Hartles had to kick dead. Parkinson, in an attempt at goal, again sent the ball dead, and another drop kick by Howard just missed. Fast play new ruled, in which Thompson, Shepherd, Parkinson, and Plumpton showed well. Plumpton got hold, and after a brilliant run, in which his opponents did not seem to have a desire to interfere, added another try to the score. Farrell kicked the last goal, and when time was called the result stood—Widnes, three goals, six minors ; Rochdale St. Clement's, two minors. Teams: Rochdale: Back, Brett (captain) ; three-quarters, Thompson, Barton, and Shepherd; half backs, Heywood, and Pilling; for- wards, W. Waugh, J. Waugh, Clegg, Oddie, B. Rideough, Lord, R. Rideoug,h, Whitehead, and Farrow. Widnes: Back, Hartlea ; three-quarters, Plumpton, Parkinson, and Clarke ; half backs Howard and Farrell; forwards, Kiddie, Hughes, Gandy, Williams, Hardman, Hewitt, Barber, Pennington, and Smith. itt;NCORli v. Vicroula thavintsim—A match under the above title was played on the Owens College ground, Fallovrfield, near Manchester, on Wednesday, in fine weather. Runcorn had a good team, and as the 'Varsity were stongly represented, an even game was expected. From the kick off, however, the Cheshire men had the match well in hand, and won very easily indeed. Run- corn went away with a good rush, but Thorpe and N. Green were instrumental in relieving to beyond half-way flag, whore Hughes got hold and passed wide to Wain- wright, who affected a most brilliant run in. Brazondale took tho place,. but was not successful. The 'Varsity were still pressed, and Broady almost got in , causing Harvey to touch down. Hastings here made a long kick, and as Thorpe followed suit, and E. J. Greene dribbled on, the visitors were slightly pressed, but Hughes, getting hold, throw out wide to Wainwright, who cantered in behind to secure Runcorn's second try • Braz.eedale again failing 1 at the place kick. Some goodkicking between Hastings and Brazendale followed, and a fine dribble by E. J. Greene almost resulted in a score for the 'Varsity. The Runcorn men soon altered the complexion of the play when Hughes threw to Woods, who, after clearing the j scrummage, ran right in and landed a goal. The home team worked hard, but were unable to prevent Hughes getting the ball away to Woods, who, when he came to the full back, threw to Hughes, who easily sailed in between the posts. Woods landed a second goal from the place. Still pressing on, Runeorn were nearly scor- ing again, but Thorpe came to the rescue with a fine bit of play. Faulkner then threw forward, and spoiled a Food chance, and Thorpe, Itil`Dougall, and N. Greene indulged in some excellent passing, which brought about half time. The home players had the benefit of the what wind was blowing upon chang- Ing ends, but it availed them little, and very soon the Runcorn captain, dodging his opponents, easily ran in, but the goal total was not increased. Some capital kicking between Harvey and Green from the 'Varsity, and Faulkner and Woods, for the Clieehiremen, was applauded, but the home team were then twice compelled to touch down, by some fumbling by Hastings enabled Broady to secure another try, and Brazendale landed a goal from a rather difficult angle. During the remainder of the game the 'Varsity men•played up well, taqng the ball almost the length of the ground on one occasion, whilst Hastings, Greet', and Thorpe all made

strong runs, but the Runcorn men always held the upper hand, and Hughes, dodging his men grr a ay, obtained a most creditable try, leaving Rone3rn winners by three goals, four tries, and four mu t er3 to nil. The losers played a fairly good game, lut showed little combination, and in this pa, ticuldx formed a distinct contrast to their opponents who pass splendidly. H. Hughes the Runcorn captain, played a very fine game, and Hughes, a hand in every try scored. Woods also did well; and Wainwright who generally plays forward, showed both speed and skill at three- quarters. Brazendale kicked well ; and forward, Gayter, Faulkner, Riley, and Broady were very prominent. For the losers the full-back, Harvey, kicked well, but was weak at tackling. Hastings was not very dangercais, and we have seen N. Green play better; but Thorpe showed up uncommonly well, and is the most promising half-back we have seen for some time. Teams:— Runcorn.—J. Brazendale, back; W. Riley, J. Woods, at.d G. T. Wainwright, three-quarters; H. Hughes and W. Evans, half-backs; W.' Faulkner, P. Riley, J. Gayter, F. Hancock, W. shaw, W. Broady, J. Bowyer W. Stubbs, and R. Dolan, forwards. University.—g. C. Harvey (Owens), back ; P. McDougall, N. Green, and W. Hastings (Owens), three-quarters • P S. Thorpe and W. Cavendish (Owens), half-backs ; Edgecombe (Univers- ity College, Liverpool), H. Campbell (Yorkshire College, Leeds), and if. K. Birley, J. Entwistle, J. Tait, W. P. Montgomery, E. J. Greene, A. M`Dougall, and A. Dreschfeld (Owens), forwards. Referee: Mr. A. M. Crooke (Lancashire County). WARRINGTON " A " •. ARDWICK IST.—Played on Satur- day, at Ardwick, under the old rules. Warrington were without the services of Jolley and Appleton, whilst Ard- wick had put their best team in the field, it being a benefit match in aid of the parents of one of their players who died some time ago whilst playing in one of their matches. Thirties being agreed upon, and Adam- son winning the toss, Morns kicked off for Ardwick, Bibby returning to centre, Donohue and Adamson headed a dribble up the field, play restinc, close on the home line. A scrimmage was formed', but Ardwick relieved pressure slightly. The Warrington forwards worked the ball over the line, a minor resulting. Barber dropped out, his kick being charged down, and a scrimmage being formed close to the home line, Lawless passed to Speakman, who kicked to touch. From the line out, Cheethani got hold and kicked to Boscow, who returned well into touch. A scrimmage was next formed OR the Ardwick line. Paine relieved by a good kick to centre. Ardwick took the ball to the Warring- ton 25, but it was quickly brought back to neutral territory. Holt was here allowed a free kick for a fair catch. Speakman returned to their quarters. From a scrimmage the visitors' forwards rushed the ball over their opponents' line, enabling Donohue to score a good try, Warburton failing at goal. Morris dropped out; Speakman returned splendidly to the home 25. From a line out Adamson got in a good kick, and a scrimmage was formed under the goal posts, where Mather passed to Speakman, who rushed over and grounded the ball, adding another try to the Warnngton score. Warburton made a very good attempt for goal. From a pack Cheetham got a pass and made away, but unfortunately knocked the bail forward. Warburton Molyneaux, Holmes, and Hayes, dribbled the ball down the field, Holt saving. Barnes got a pass, and put in a good kick over the home line, but the ball was ruled back for some infringement. Skinner next made a good run and carried play to centre, but the Warrington forwards rushed the ball back to Ardwick quarters, the ball going dead, a minor resulting. Bibby replied to the drop out, and Ardwick were awarded another free kick for a foul charge. Bibby failing to rcturn' caused play to rest in the centre. A grand dribble, headed by' Hayes, Holmes, Adamson, and Ratcliffe took play to Ardwick territory, Holmes completing the try. which Warburton converted into a goal. Half-time was now called, the score being 1 goal, 2 tries, and 2 minors to nil. On change of ends, Warburton kicked off for the visitors. Cheetham returned, play resting in centre. The Ardwick forwards broke away with a dribble, Speakman saving. Shortly afterward the home forwards rushed away to the Warrington 25, causing Boscow to touch down. Ashurst dropped out. Parkinson returned to Warburton, who kicked well into touch in centre, where play raged for some time. Paine got in a good into touch. up the field, Boscow replying by a long kick touch. The home forwards took play to the Warrington 25, and Barnes relieved by a good kick into touch. From the line-out the Warrington forwards, headed by Ashurst, Holmes, and Ratcliffe, rushed the oval to Ard- wick 25. A scrimmage was formed, and Mather getting hold and feigning to pass, got away with a nice tricky run, but was tackled close to the line. From the scrim- mage the Warrington forwards rushed over and forced a minor. Barnes afterwards got a pass, and made a nice run up the field, but was tackled by Holt. Holmes, Beard, Adamson, and Ashurst dribbled well to the home 25, and later, play was carried to the Ardwick line, Warburton getting over, but the try was disallowed. A scrimmage was formed five yards from the line. One of the Warrington men (Lawless) beim,' hurt caused the spectators to encroach on the ground, which stopped further play ten minutes from call of time, the score standing as follows :—Warrington 1 goal, 2 tries, and 3 minors, to Ardwick 1 minor. Teams :—Warrington : J. Boscow' full back; 11. Bibky, J. Speakman, and A. Barnes, three-quarter backs; J. Lawless and S. Mather, half backs; W. Hayes, T. Donohue, W. Warburton, C. R. Adamson (captain), A. Molyneaux, A. Ratcliffe, G. Beard, J. Holmes, and J. Ashurst, forwards. Ard- wick: S. Hall, full backs ; J. W. Paine, T. Holt, and J. Cheetham, three-quarter back ; J. C. Broadfoot and H. Skinner, half backs ; F. J. Barber (captain), H. Morriss, E. Webster W. Walker, J. Simpson, E. Doodson, T. Wood, M. Webster, and J. Sellers, forwards. WARRINGTON V. WAKEFIELD TRINITY._

This match, the most important fixture en the Warrington card, was brought to an issue on Saturday, when fully 5,000 football enthusiasts assembled to witness the encounter. For some time past the meeting has been eagerly discussed, and speculation was rife as to the ultimate result. Many were of opinion that, taking into consideration the recent brilliant victories of the " wirepullers " over Kendal Hornets and Askam, the Tykes would have all their work cut out to administer defeat to the home team, whilst not a few pinned their faith on the capabilities of the Warring- tonians in coming out of the fray victorious. Both teams were loudly cheered on making their appearance. Dillon, the home skipper, who had been operating in county matches for the past three weeks, on taking his place in the team, attired in his county cap and jersey, met with a hearty recepdon. Jolley was still absent from the Warrington side, whilst with regard to Wake- field, Fotherby and J. H. Jones were conspicuous by their absence. .

Latham, the Wakefield captain, chose to defend the railway goal, Frank Turner starting operations, Lowrie replying in touch at half way. The first to show up were Antrobus and Speakman, who with neat passing took the oval to the Wakefield quarter flag. A free kick for a "knock on" was claimed by Fallas, and again neutral ground was the scene of operations. Massey here punted to Brannan and the latter mulling allowea Ashton to rush up and place thevisiting goal in jeopardy. A rush by the home forwards took the leather apparently over the line, Dillon grounding, but the oval was ruled back. This decision was not relished at all by the Warringtonians, and Mr. Beswick's ruling hardly met with favour. However, relief was brought about by Fallas taking advantage of awild pass to Massey, but the latter neutralized whatever advantage had been gained by ' a timely kick to half way. Whiteley and Binks here became prominent by a capital bribble, Evans only getting the oval away in the nick of time. Speakman and Antrobus passed accurately, and a long pass to Hulme was nicely. intercepted by Daniels, the ball ultimately going in touch at the quarter flag. A combined dribble by the Tykes now placed the Warring- tonians on the defensive. Povey was am lauded for an effort, and later on Frank Turner grassed Hutchinson when the latter was becoming dangerous. Exchange kicks by Barnes and Brennan were next witnessed but from a line out Lowrie secure possession, and effected a dashing run in, Whiteley making a good bid for goal. Frank Turner depped out, and for a time the play was a give-and- take nature' until the monotony was relieved by the fine pressing of the Wakefield backs, which ultimately ended in Fallas getting over, though to all appearance he had been held quite safe before he grounded. The referee, however, decided against the Warringtonians, and Whiteley took the place without success. Warrington now improved in their play, when it seemed that there was a chance of equalizing,Harrison stopped the progress of the Warrington forwards by a huge punt to the War- rington quarter flag. Massey, Frank Turner, and Dillon were applauded tor their efforts, and after Dunn had put in a useful kick to the Warrington line Evans saved, and half-time was called with the score—Wakefield, 2 tries 1 minor; Warrington nil Booth restarted, and a free kick to Warrington took play to the Tykes' quarter flag. Time after time the home forwards broke away only to have their efforts frustrated by the well-judged kicks of the Yorkshire backs. Daniels was severely tested at this point of the game, but managed to check the career of his weightier opponents. The brothers Turner came .through the pack, and Antrobus ' endeavoured to steal away, only to find a barrier in Whiteley. Pack scrimmages were the chief order, tint play being confined to the forwards. This fact was attributable to the Yorkshire team adhering to the old rule of wing forwards. and loud werekhe comments on their adopting this style of play. After Barnes had cleared his lines, Maks compelled a a minor to be added to the Wakefield score. Dillon broke away from a line out, leading his team in gallant style, hut te no purpose. The superior back play of the visitors proved a tower of strength to their side, and altougk they strove hard to force an opening, the Warrington defence was not to be tampered with. Only minor points were scored, and as the play was chiefly of a forward nature, comment is out of the question. The latter portion of the game was played in semi- darkenness, and when the whistle was blown for no-side, the telegraph board read as follows :—Wakefield Trinity, two tries, five minors ; Warrington, nil. Wakefield owed a good deal of their success to their style of playing wing forwards,which completely spoiled the efforts of the opposing half backs. But in addition to this their play all through was remarkably well-

001, ALARMING OUTBREAK OF FEVER. DEATH DEATH OF A TOWN COUNCILLOR AND .-01 EX-TOWN COUNCILLOR. hoot A painful sensation was occasioned throug- St. Helens, on Thursday morning by the annoMIS,O ment of the death, from typhoid fever, of t:ed gentlemen both widely known and highly respeCLor in the town and neighbourhood. For some " days there has been an epidemic of typhoid and several gentlemen occupying prominent poi; tions in the town have been affected, including Peg Councillor John Lowe and Mr. William Longtoo ex-town councillor, both of whom died on Thurso - morning, the former at half-past two and the at eight o'clock. Mr. Lowe's case is t sudden. He was in town so late as Sat, last, and it was not known even among colleagues in the Council that he was ill till the ' man of the Health Committee announced it at the L ing on Wednesday afternoon, and expressed a hoPe his speedy recovery. He was first returned tptieg Council Chamber in November, 1885, as a Conserva, for West Sutton, astd re-elected without opposition month. He was deputy chairman of the school At, dance Committee, and for many years a member Prescot Board of Guardians, of which body he was c"" man last year. He lived at Elton Head Farm, Bei belonging to the Marquis of Salisbury. He was 45 years of age, and leaves a widow and family to lake' his untimely end. He was attended by Dr. Gas Mr. Wm. Longton. who resided at Eccleston Grangefil, also been in the Council a couple of years, but reti7ive 1887. He was one of the founders of the Conser/k Club, and took a prominent part in the liamentary election for the Newton Division, ing assiduously for the Conservative cause Eccleston district. He wasa self-made man, and on business as a quarry master. Up to last a when hesevered his connection, he was agent for Hughes, and latterly had been agent for the estate. Dr. Garton had been attending him. greatest possible sympathy i 3 on all hands exly the widow and children of both the deceased in their affliction. Mr. Thomas Walker, another ex-town councillor, is being attended by Dr. M‘Nicoll. is also seriouslf s' ing from typhoid. His doctor pronounces tb° "serious but hopeful." There are about ten, cases in the town, and among those who are s0.„1 are Mr. J. O. Swift, solicitor ; Mr. William Jo Cook, ironfounder, Atlas Foundry, and residing at villas; and Mr. Ernest Baxter, copper smelter caustic manufacturer, Parr, residing at Bainhill. on all sides is entertained that they may be .1 restored to health, but Thursday morning's sad gence made their friends exceedingly anxious.

Cassell and Co - . 310175 E COMMITTEE. LThig Committee reported that it had examined three ;Mors for anew cast iron boiler tank at the Workhouse, 7i!lci recommended that the tender of Messrs. Pearson, Cowles, and Co. be accepted at £l2O nett.—Mr. eliarowproposed the adoption of he minutes, and Mr. uAREYSNIRE seconded the proposal.—Mr. JOLLEY moved kan amendment that the tender of the Widnes Foundry . oat £lO5, allowing £1 for the old tank, be accepted ;Object te the completion of work within four weeks Mtn delivery.--Mr. BLACKHURST seconded the proposal. ;--It was s ated that the other tender was that of Messrs. ones and Son at £l2B 10s., £.5 to be allowed for the 1,81 tank.—After a considerable amount of discussion, "tr. Jolley's amendment was accepted byls votes to 6. THE CHRISTMAS DINNER:—MORE BEER. ji Mr. Gamin's° proposed that the inmates of the Work- ,?ase have on Christmas day a dinner consisting of roast "ef and plum pudding, as they had had for many years. Hearcor said he would second the proposal that the Inniatos have their usual Christmas dinner.—Mr. GREEN- IX(4 said that was hardly seconding his proposal; he did tat say the " usual " Christmas dinner.—Mr. HEATON !,aiCI he meant the usual dinner, that was that the inmates mould have the usual quantity of beer.—Mr. CLARKE Beconded Mr. Greening's proposition.—Mr: HEATON then Itved that the inmates of the house have their usual hristrnas dinner.—Mr. HIBBERT seconded this proposal. 1--t-lilr. JOLLEY' suggested that the female inmates only ilaye half a pint of leer instead of a pint, and Mr. ~i.roir accepted this suggestion.—Mr. BLACKHORST said plat after the scenes that were witnessed in that , Work- at last Christmas, such as people scaling the walls, 'Co he thought there ought to be some limit set 1131 P. He was not opposed to people having a glass of beer, et he thought sorne.lirnit ought to be put to it. In some eft,ses females who did not take beer at all handed it "el' to the next person the consequence being that ~.,4SII, t, Pt %IMP got 'lilt() a beistly state of drunkenness, 'mien, IS MIT One liiieve, almost brought disgrace on the Union.—Mr. Diatiiirrinnie supported. Mr. Gre,ening's Proposal, and said that he believed if the Master and Matron's opinions were asked they ' would both be against beer being given.—Mr. Rescuyes said he did tot see any drunkenness on last Christmas day at the. Workhouse.—Mr. Marxism; believed that Christmas Was scarcely Christmas unless people -had' some eithile- ratingbeverage, and, therefore, wpported the amend- -!oent.—The CHAIRMAN Suggeste'd that they might have, 'die opinion of the Workhouse master, but Mr. JOLLEY Objected to this proposal as, he said, that was entirely a Matter for the Guardians to decide.—Mr. Isnenwoon Said the Workhouse master last year was carrying out the instructions of the Board, but Mr, Jolley insisted ilPon his giving the inmates a little more beer.—Mr. ' JOLLEY said that was untrue. He said that the beer that was to be given the inmates was a .pint each, but '.sorne one had gone and interfered and given them half a A Pint, and he objected to it, and insisted upon -the instructions of the Board being carried out. . --Mr. Isasawoon said that in the presence , of the inmates Mr. Jolley insisted upon more beer being given to them.—Mr. JOLLEY : I insisted upon each one flaying a pint.—Mr. BLACKILITEST said he hoped the ' Wia.ster would be allowed to carry out the instructions of the Board, and that no member of the Board would be 'allowed to interfere with him. (Hear, hear.)—The ' Wommouss MASTER said that last year he was under the impression that the instructions of the Board were that each inmate was to have half a pint of beer and he ' served out that quanti y, but it appeared that he had 'M. ade a mistake, and when Mr. Jolley came he told him was the instruction of the Board that the inmates _Should have a pint each. He, therefore, gave them each ...another half-pint. He only gave beer to those who , asksd for it. The drunkenness, he added, was not so '. Much due to the beer - the people got in the workhouse, as about 70 or 80 went out to public worship and their ': , friends treated elem.—Mr. GREENING- said *that Whether Mr. limacliffe did or di,d not see any drunken- ' bees at the workhouse last Christmas Day it ' 'WU the fact that there was drunkenness. Half a ' dozen women were so drunk that nothing could be * done with them, and they got out of the dining hall, and, having scaled the walls, rambled about outside until the next day they were brought up before the borough bench for being drunk and incapable. (Hear, hear.) He thought it was an absolute piece of cruelty to the inmates to giye them beer. ("No, no.") There was not a gentleman there but knew that.seven-eighths '3f the male inmates of workhouses at all events came ' there through drink,either directly or indirectly. There ' were men in the workhouse who formerly held good - Positions in society, and who hadi been brought there entirely through drink, and now the would at the Christmas season again whet their appetites for more.— The CHAIRMAN agreed with Mr. Greening that the ', majority of the poor people were brought to that work- house through the intemperate habits they had formed outside. Drink was the curse that was the ruin of the , Population of this country. He believed that this was 1' the most drunken country in Europe, and that was a l'ery serious charge to lay at their door. The c induct of the inmates in previous years formed a decided argument with him for leading him to the conclusion to support the motion. They knew that the facilities afforded them by that Board for getting drunk had been abused. ' lie really thought it was not right that they, should so ' Persistently and wilfully put in the way of the working, classes so many temptations to drink. They had public houses in their towns almost door to door, and anyone coming sober from, say, Liverpool to Warrington, had temptation on his right hand and his left and all the Way along. He should certainly vote against drink being given to the inmates of the Workhouse.—A vote was then taken and 13 voted in favour of the amendment that I)e.er be given and six against, the amendment, therefore, °Nag carried. This concluded the business of public importance. ,

I Sir,—Allow me through- the medium of your valuable columns to add my testimony to that of "A Sufferer," and I should like also to draw the attention of The Paving Committee to the bad state of the footpath along Knutsford-road. What with loose tiles, and holes where tiles should be, it is no uncommon thing if you should happen to tread on a loose tile for the mud to fly on you as high as your knees. Only last Sunday night a lady was going to church, and, not being able to see these holes, happened to tread in one, and it almost threw her down, besides filling her boot full of water.—Yours, &c., F. B. j

CHRISTMAS DINNER TO THE POOR CHILDRDEN. Sir,—lt has been the custom for several years past for the Mayor to arrange for a dinner to the poor children of Warrington on Christmas Day. I hope his Worship will not let the fact that work is slightly Letter in town interfere with so deserving an objeCt. Warrington may be better off than it has been for a few years, but there are great numbers to whom a good dinner is a luxury, and I for one shall be very pleased to contribute towards the cast of the dinner. I trust the Mayor will take the hint, and let the banks open an account to meet the expense, for I am fully convinced there are many who would be pleased thus to show their SYMPATHY.

COUNTY COUNCILS. Increasing interest is being taken in the forth- coming elections, and fresh candidates are announced daily. The last day for receiving nominations in Lancashire is -Monday, the 7th January, and the polling in the contested divisions will take place on the 15th of the same month. The places at which nominations are to be received have notbeen fixed in all cases, but it may be assumed that in Local Board districts where such districts are coextensive with the electoral divisions, the nominations will be receivcd at the Local Board offices; in other cases the most convenient centres will be chosen, and due notification will be given by the return- ing officer to all concerned. The functionstof the returning officer (the High Sheriff of the county) do not extend to those divisions which are coexten- tive with boroughs divided into wards, or comprised in such boroughs but coextensive with wards. This fact, which indicates an omission in the framing of the Act, having been brought under the notice of the Local Government Board, a circular has been issued directing the mayors of such boroughs—or persons to be appointed by them—to act as return- ing officers. This order applies in the case of Lancashire to 13 boroughs—namely, Warrington, which sends three member.;; Damen, Bacup, Accrington. Ashton-under-Lyne, and Southport, which send two members each: and Lancaster, Chorley, Clitheroe, Blackpool, Mossley, Heywood, and Middleton. which send one member each to the County Council. It seems not to be generally known that the expenses which a candidate may legally incur in the promotion of his election sre limited by the Municipal Elections (Corrupt Practices) Act, 1884, which is incorporated with the Local Government Act. The maximum amount to be spent in a con- stituency of 2,000 voters is ..£3l ss.—that is to say, £25 for the first 500 voters and 3d. per voter for the remainder. A return of the expenses actually incurred must be sent by each candidate to the Clerk to the Council within 28 days after the election. The use of committee-rooms, hired con- veyances, kc., is likewise governed by the Act of 1884. For the former purpose public-houses, or clubs where intoxicating liquors are sold, are strictly forbidden. One committee-room may be hired for every 2,000 voters, apart from places , gratuitously placed at the disposal of candidates, upon which there is no limitation. The same restrictions apply as in boroughs with regard to the emplOyment of clerks and paid agents.

div.head: FALSE TEACHING IN FRODSHAM.
div.p: FALSE TEACHING IN FRODSHAM.

Sir,—On Saturday last I got hold of the parish maga- zine, November "Banner of Faith," and, in page 264, I read as follows:—" What is your name? N. or M.? We don't want your surname, by which you are known in this world, but your Christian name, which is written in heaven. Baptism stamps you for the kingdom of heaven. Holy Baptism washes away original sin, in which you were born by descent from Adam. We are brothers and sisters by Baptism with all the saints in earth and in Paradise, therefore we may glory in our nobility. Let us promote Baptism with all our power and love."

After reading above, is there any wonder at so many sceptics existing? It is such trash as this which tends to keep people from going to a place of worship; no need, according to this, for prayers and sermons or' expositions of the Scriptures. But what saith the greatest Teacher the world ever had? "Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you. SaTctify them through Thy truth; Thy word is truth." And St. Paul says "In Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the Gospel "(see John, se. 24v.; 15c. 3v.; 17c. 17v.; I. Cor. 4c. 15v. ; Rom. 10c. 17v.). Faith. hope, and charity; but pure faith first, then Peace, but the latter may be bought at too dear a price by sacrificing truth. It is tho duty of all Protestants to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints. Who are the people doing harm? Circulators of teaching leading step by step to Rome. Let me ask your readers not to be led away with such rubbish as is in this magazine. Daily sell ;cad and missions are useless where pernicious literature follows. ROBERT FOULKES. Frodsham, Dec. sth, 1888.

THE TEMPERANCE QUESTION. Sir,—l should feel obliged if you could find space in your paper for a few remarks on the hotter which appeared in your las issue, by "W. Furness." lam surprised that he should write to your paper such a letter when your paper took such a noble part in expos- ing the fallacy and injustice of the Compensation Clauses. It is quite evident from his letter that he is totally ignorant of the discussion which took place throughout the country, and defeated the object of the Government, in seeking to pass a measure which has never been supported by the Tories, only on the ground that it was an honest attempt to settle a complicated question. I am also surprised that he should take to himself the task of teaching others about what he knows next to nothing himself. He states that they opposed a measure which had for its object the giving the people permission to buy up any Public-house or dram-shop which they thought useless. Now, sir, I say that is totally inaccurate. What they opposed was making a license into a vested interest, which you, sir, took such pains to explain to the people of Warrington, when the contro- versv was before the public. Then he states that the Temperance party consider a few thousand pounds of more consequence than the social and moral welfare of 'heir fellow-creatures. Here as:ain he shows lamentabie ignorance, for he ought to have known it was millions that were at stake, to compensate, not men who would have to give up a livine, but a body of brewers, who have already amassed great fortunes out of the misery of their fellow-creatures. I should not wonder, sir, if "W Furness" would not have called our Saviour " a fanatic," and" robber" for throwing those who "bought and sold," out of the temple, that is if he had been alive in those days. If "W. Fulness "wants to teach us, let him show us first, by fact and argument, that the drink traffic is a benefit to mankind. The last part of his letter deserves attention. Our Coffee-houses are not what they oue,ht to be, we know; but counsel from such an enemy to temperance comes with very bad grace indeed.—Yours, J. HORTON. 18, Catherine-se., Warrington, Dec. 6th, 1888..

div.head: CHESHIRE FARMERS AND THE ELECTIONS.
div.p: CHESHIRE FARMERS AND THE ELECTIONS.

On Wednesday evening another meeting-of farmers, for the most part belonging to Cheshire, was held at the Farmers' Stores, Bewsey-st., Warrington, under the auspices of the Farmers' Club, to further consider the selection of candidates to the County Council who will be favourable to the interests of the farming community. Since the club took action some three weeks ago, a number of farmers' candidates have accepted invitations to be put in nomination, and have issued addresses to the voters of the various electoral divisions. As a result, it is more than probable that there will be a considerable number of contested elections in the districts embraced by the membership of the club. Mr. Thomas Newton
