On Monday a meeting of Parochial Authorities and ' fanners was held at the Nag's Head Hotel, Warrington, , when a deputatien was appointed to wait upon Mr. J. C. Sutton, (clerk to the Warrington Board of Guardians) at Bewsey Chambers, to request him to become a candi- date for the representation of the St inwick District on the County Council.—Mr. Lowe (Rixton Hall) saia the gentlemen present were deputed by a meeting ef honor- ary overseers and largo farmers of the townships in the Winwick District to communicate to him (Mr. Sutton) their unanimous request that he would undertake the representation of their interests on the new County Council. They had considered the matter over in all its bearings, and his knowledge and experience of local and county business induced the meetingto make the request. —Mr. Sutton, in the course of a speech that he then delivered, referred to his connection with parochial business, and to the management of union and rural , government. In conclusion he said that a conference would shortly be held, and notably attended by other local administrators and ratepayers. If after then he should be the candidate, so soon as his existing engage- ments would permit, he would probably meet the electors and explain bayond what he had then deemed it necessary to say.—Several of the deputation here expressed the hope that Mr. Sutton would enable them to say he had given his consent, but Mr. Surrox he felt sure he could not with proprie y or courtesy to others saymore until the conference.—The deputation then withdrew. THE WINWICK DIVISION.—CONFERENCE AT WARRINGTON. After the meetings of the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority and Assessment Committee a conference was held yesterday afternoon In the Board-room, Warrington Workhouse, for the purpose of considering the represent- ation of the Winwick division on the Lancashire County Council. The Rev. G. F. Roberts, chairman of the Rural Sanitary Authority,was elected to the chair,and amongst those present were several members of the Rural Sanitary Authority, overseers and assistant overseers, and others. The Chairman said it was very necessary that they should select a gentleman who would fairly well represent the division, and who could deal I with the difficulties that would no doubt face the County I Council during at any rate the first few years of its I existence. He had a suggestion to make. He was con- fident they could net have a better man to representthem in the County Council than Mr. Sutton. He thought Mr. Sutton was in every way competent to fulfil the duties of the office, and to give satisfaction if elected. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Pennington (Winwick) thought that if they elected Mr. Sutton to represent them they should not only do something useful for the County Council but do honour to themselves. He was quite sure Mr. Sutton was able te take a leading part in the business of the new Council. There had been another gentleman nominated for the Winwick division but not, according to the names in the papers, by Lancashire men but by Cheshire men. He had always thought, that Lancashire men were capable of conducting their own business and of choosing for themselves. (Hear, hear.) He moved that Mr. Sutton be invited to allow himself to be nominated as a candidate for the Winwick —Mr. Cooper (Winwick) seconded this proposal.— Mr. John Itylands in supporting it, said that Mr. Sutton was eminently fitted to represent them on the County Council.—Mr. W. Houghton also spoke in favour of the proposal.—Mr. W. Darbyshire said he wished to explain with regard to the statement that they were all Cheshire people at the meeting of the Farmers' Club which nominated Mr. Warburton,that the gentleman who seconded the proposal to nominate Mr. Warburton lived In Lancashire.—The motion in favour of Mr. Sutton's candidature was ,hen put to the meeting and there were thirteen votes in favour of it. Only one or two hands were held up against, and it was, therefore, declared to be carried.—ln acknowledging the vote Mr. Sutton said he would accept their invitation. He ta ;shed to point out that if he were returned he would no,, person- ally, be benefitted in the smallest degree. He should have expenses to pay ont of his own Docket, and many duties to -discharge for which 1116 Voted Pet receive any compeneation whatever. (Hear, hear.) If Mr. Warburton and he went to the electors and If Mr. Warburton were re urned he (Mr. Sutton) would simply be relieved of a large amount of responsibility, and, in some cases, perhaps of some anxiety. He was sure that he and Mr. Warburton would remain good friends throughout the contest, and that their discussions would be confined to the public business of the county. (Hear. hear.) THE WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB AND THE CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. Speaking at the annual meeting of the Lymm Con- stitutional Association, on Tuesday evening, Mr. Peter Stubs, J.P., allrded to the coming election of the Cheshire County Council and the part which was being taken in it by the political associations in the district. It had been the desire of the Liberals that Mr. John D. Dewhtirst should be asked both by them and the Conservatives, but he had been told some months ago that Mr. Dewhurst declined to stand, and intimated that he should vote for Mr. Charles Lister, who seemed to the Conservatives a most suitable candidate. The Warrington Farmers' Association had, however, seen fit to select a candidate, but had most properly refused to make their selection on political grounds. Unfortu- nately, he feared they were to have a contest, with all its attendant cost to the county and the candidates. Individually he respected the feelings of the farmers that as large ratepayers they ought to be represented, though he could not but think that they would be more efficiently represented by Mr. Charles Lister—(applause) —who was well acquainted with all the forms of pro- cedure, and who would be more able than an un' rained man could be to get for farming matters the attention they deserved. However, he trusted it might be possible to conduct the contest without any political rancour, and that the result Might show the wisdom of the choice of the constituency. The new Council would need a number of good men to conduct its deliberations Into correct and orderly channsls, and he hoped with the innate spirit ef fair play which characterized Englishmen. County Councils might be made into valuable institutions for the benefit °Mite country at 'ange. (Applause.) APPLETON DIVISION. On Tuesday evenine'a public meeting of the electors In the Appleton Division was held in the large room, Grappenhall, to consider the selection of a candidate for the division in the Cheshire County Council. Mr. Edward Greenall presided, and was supported by Mr. Charlton Parr, Mr. Robert Davies, Mr. John Cliffe, Mr' R. H. Kerr. and Mr. H. Greenall. Amongst the audience were the Rev. Canon Greenall, Major Litton, Mr. Lyster Kaye, Mr. Vera Davies. Mr. R. J. Wynne-Jones, Mr. H. J. Longton, Mr. John Tinsley. Mr. James Cliffe, Mr. Y't Pearson, Mr. C. J. Calvert, Mr. George Fairhurst, jun., and several ladies. The Chairman, at the outset, read a telegram he had received from Mr. Naylor, regretting that business from home prevented his attendance, but wishing Mr. Charlton Parr's candidature success. (Applause.) A letter had also been received from Mr. Wm. Long regretting that a prior engagement took him to London that night : but if present he could only have reiterated the views he had stated more fully elsewhere, that a meeting of delegates from each township ought to be called. He (the Chairman) said so far as his experi- ence went, it was not everyone who was qualified to give the time and cost of the next two or three years to carry- ing on the duties of a county councillor. It rested with them to do their duty, and return a suitable representa- tive. He believed that in the townships of. Appleton there were 7,523 inhabitants, aid he thought they should obtain a proper representation. (Applause.)— Mr. J. Cliffe proposed " That this meeting is of opinion that J. C. Parr, Esq., is a fit and proper person to repre- sent the Appleton Division of Cheshire on the County Council, and pledges itself to use every legitimate effort to secure his triumphant 'return. (Applause.)—Mr. Robert Davies seconded the proposition. He believed that two candidates had issued their addresses, but he thought that Mr. Parr, who had been brought up amongst figures, was a man whom they ought to send as their representative, and he had very great pleasure in seconding his nomination.—Mr.Calvert supported the resolution, observing that the electors resident in Stock- ton Heath and Wilderspool would, almost to a man, support Mr. Parr. (Applause.)—The Chairman put the resolution to the meeting, and it was carried by an Over- whelming majority, only one hand, that of Mr. John Darbyshire (Stretton), being held up against it.— Mr. Darbvshire Said he might as well tell them openly and candidly that he did not think their friend and neighbour Mr. Parr was the best man to represent the !Appleton Division in the County Council. He thought Mr. Parr was really too high up to be a representative for them, and lived too much in the centre of a valuable Park to be able to judge of the requirements of the larger number of the electors in the division.—Mr. Charlton Parr then returned thanks for his selectionby the meeting.—Mr. Darbyshire said Mr. Parr had very kindly thrown himself open to have questions asked him by the electors. Addressing Mr. Parr he asked: Do you, Mr. Parr, think that the County Council of Cheshire should be composed of men of *ll CIAMPS, say farmers and labourers. or do you not? (A Voice "I should say not.")—Mr. Parr: I should leave that entirely to the electors, whoever they thought proper to send up to the Council. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Darbyshire: lam asking you for your opinion.—Mr. Parr: It is not a question of opinion, but of fact—Mr. Darbyshire (resuming his seat): It is net a convenient time to answer that question, I suppose.—A vote of thanks was then accorded the Chair- man.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

ACCIDENT AT ACTON GRANGE. About four o'clock last evening a fireman employed on the Acton Grange Section of the Canal was taken on a locomotive to the hospital at Latchford. He was believed to have been jumpieg off the engine, and to have clipped, his foot being caught under the wheel. We understand that he is now progressing favourably. RUNCORN. Work is progressing steadily on this section at No Man's Land. A large number of steel rail piles have been driven, to fdrin a qoffer dam and in a few days the foun- dation for a portion of the river wall will be put in. A portable engine and pump is now on the spot in order to pump water from the coffer dam, and several rafts are in course of construction to aid in the general works. The high tides of the past few .days have impeded the operations to some extent. MOORE TO STOCKTON HEATH. The contractor has not been able to take the fullest advantaged the recent mild weather owing to the flood- ing of the cutting in several parts of the sections. The pumping engines are kept going night and day and the water so long as the rain keeps off, is steadily decreasing. The railway embankment at Acton Grange is still increasing in height and forms a prominent feature in the view of that part of the cutting. The mission work is steadily kept up and is fully appreciated by the navvies and their families. In consequence of a com- plaint made by Mr. Charlton Parr that locomotives passing under Twenty Step Bridge, are liable to cause accidents by high ening horses on the road above, a boarding has been erected on each side of the road, which keeps from the view of anyone on the road, anything that passes on the rails beneath. It is also sta- ed that the boarding prevents mischievous persons from throwing at the engines, etc., which pass under the bridge. The German navvy is completing its excavation at a rapid rate, filling a train of more than a score of waggons in little more than half an hour.

LATCHFORD, THELWALL, &c. 'the head of the cutting at Latchford is as busy as can be, a large number of men working full time there. There are to American navvies at work, and the cutting lengthens rapidly. The pumps have not just here been required so much as in other parts of the excavation.

BARTON, Pcc. On Monday evening, at the monthly meeting of the Eccles Local Board, it was reported that plans had been submitted for the erection of a new hospital at Barton for the Ship Canal contractor, and that plans had also been submitted for the erection of 100 houses by a private owner. The deviation lines for the Cheshire Lines Railway at Irlam, and the Stockport and Glaze- brook Railway at Cadishead, are making great progress, the new embankments being already at a higher level than the existing lines.

That the Rev. W. Bryant, 8.A., B.Sc., is about to vacate his curacy at Runcorn Parish Church, in order to take an important position in a college in the South of England. That during the two years he has laboured in the town, he has won the respect and esteem of the parishioners, and his approaching departure is much regretted. That it is chiefly owing to his energy of his fostering care that the Church Institute enjoys such a vigorous existence, and it is hoped that his suc- cessor will be able to continue his work. . _ _

That there is quite a revival of the missionary spirit anaongst the Wesleyans of the neighbourhood remark caused by the fact that during the past year, the Runcorn Circuit has contributed .£5O and the Widnes Circuit £45 more than usual to the funds of the Home and Foreign Missions. That the report on the census of children pre- sented to the Runcorn School Board, on Tuesday,by the Clerk, was a very able one and contained some interesting statistics. his aparent that the boys are net so tenacious of life as the girls. The figures show that in tile earlier years the boys are much more numerious than the girls, but as the years roll, the former die off and the two sexes are on an equality, when the age of 13 is reached. At 20 one would suppose the girls will be in a great majority. That at the conclusion of the ordinary business of the Board of Commissioners, on Thursday, the members resolved themselves into Committee and discussed a matter of deep interest to the ratepayers with closed doors. It is said. That Mr. E. Imison, chairman of the Finance Committee, explained that not only had the Assess- ment Committee of the Union thrown expense upon the ratepayers by their ill-advised attempt to in- crease the assessment of the Bridgewater Under- taking of the Ship Canal Company, but they had done Runcorn a special injustice by agreeing to an alteration in the basis of the assessment which would mean a loss of about .£l3O a year to the rate- payers of the town. That this is nearly equal to one penny in the .£ on the rates, and a lively scene followed this revelation. That the question ought to be pressed home " Who is responsible to the Board of Commissioners for this gross neglect of the interests of Runcorn." That two votaries of the flower that blooms in the spring, otherwise the Primrose League, have been making themselves very busy lately by getting up a requisition to Major Hazlehurst as'king him to become a candidate for the County Council in Runcorn North. That this attempt to foist two Tory magistrates upon the town by the "non-political dodge" has met with condemnation even from Conservatives and Major Hazleharst has given the two gentlemen, mentioned a decided rebaff by absolutely refusing to acquiesce to their" prayer." That the Liberal Council will consider the situa- tion. at a meeting to be held next week.

div.head: WIDNES AND THE -PARNELL DEFENCE
div.p: WIDNES AND THE -PARNELL DEFENCE

FUND. A public meeting, convened by the Local- Com- mittee of the Parnell Defence Fund, was held in Widners Drill Hall on ,Monday evening. The room was about three parts filled. Dr. Olieefle occupied the chair, and on the platform were Mr. S. Mahonv, M.P., Mr. McDonnell, Mr. McCambridge, 'Messrs. E. Carey; J. Morrison, B. Fox, F. Cave, and F. Heat- land.

In his opening address the Chairman alluded to the recent Tory meeting held in that hall, and remarked that he could take objection to nothing the member for the Widnes Bivision, Mr. Moss, said. except that he was as far frora Home %Ile as aver (Hooting.) They could all see, hevrever, that the tendency of the day was most decidedly in favour of Home Rule. (Applause.) He characterised the Parnell Commission as an electioneer- ing dodge, an attempt to disgust the people of England, by brincrine, forth evidence which was simply a re-hash ef events that had been taking place for the last six or seven years, but they would never prevent England giving Home Rule to Ireland by such means as these. (Applause.) Mr. E. Carey moved "That this meeting stiongly condemns the coercive policy of the present Government. and denounces such a policy asunnecestssarv, brutal and tyrannical, and detrimental to the unity of the empire." (Applause.) Dealing with the question of rent,Mr. Carey said the greater part of our difficulties in Ireland at the present time had arisen through the refusal of the House of Commons to pass Mr. Parnell's Arrears Bill in 1888. and although the Plan of Campaign might be an illegal method rd procedure, he did not see what else the tenants of Ireland were to do. (Applause) The question of arrears was one which required settlement at the earliest Possible moment. (Applause.) The Commission appointed to inquire into the case ef the Scotch Crofters had been empowered to deal with arrears,and it appeared as if anything required in any part of the empire, except the Irish, could be granted when it was once shown that it was iustiv demanded. (Applause.) Unfortunately it seemed as if they had set their faces against the Irish people, and were determined never to do them justice if they could possibly avoid it. (Hear, hear.) But the tide was turning; they would soon be able to join in a thankful song of victory. The only way in which they could get the empire united was that given in accord- ance with the wishes of the people. (Applause.) Before long the pexmle of England would demand in their might what was the,ir right, that Ireland should be governed as England, Scotland, and Wales were. (Applause.) Mr. MORRISON seconded the resolution, and argued to show that the policy of the present Govern- ment was dangerous, and likely to bring disaster upon the country. (Applatise.) The days of coercion were numbered; a general election could not be long deferred, and when it came the people would sweep the Tory Government fromlthe face of power and replace in Its stead Mr. Gladstone, determined to do justice to Ireland. (Applause.) Mr. MARONY, M.P., supported the resolution, and, referring to the Parnell commission, said the policy of ' the " Times " appeared to be to avoid bringing direct charges against the Irish members, but to bring for- ward a re-bash of outrages and other terrible events which happened many years ago, and which they all deplored ; and which were perfectly well known in 1885, when there was a close and intimate alliance between the Tories and the Irish party. (Hear, hear.) The Tories believed they were playing a vet g good card, and that the re-hash of outrages was having an enormous influence upon the country. He did not believe anything of the kind, and in the Holborn division, where the Law Courts were situated, the Liberals had reduced the majority against them by 800 votes. (Applause.) He believed before this inquiry was ended they would find that so far from doing the Irish cause harm, it would do them the greatest possible good. (Applause.) Ile understood that the proprietor of the "Times" pinned his faith upon the forged letters. So did he (Mr. Mahony) and he re.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Thursday. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also present the Rev J. W. N. Tanner; Messrs. Knowles, Hewitt, Smith, Whit- low, Tayl r, Aaron, Brandreth, Stokes, Weir, Speak- man, Catnpkin, Once, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).—The workhouse master (Mr. Cunnah) reported that Mr. J. Robinson, ef Aston, had given a magic lantern entertainment to the children and adults in the dining ball, and, on the motion of the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, a vote of thanks was awarded Mr. tobinson.—The rest of the busines was formal.

div.head: SHIP CANAL MINSTRELS AT WESTO-N
div.p: SHIP CANAL MINSTRELS AT WESTO-N

POINT. On Monday evening, a nigger minstrel troupe composed chiefly of gentlemen in the employ of the Ship Canal Co. gave an entertainment in the Church salmi, Weston Point. Although the weather was most unfavourable so great was the interest attached to the affair that long before the time advertised to start, the room was crowded, and many people had to return to their homes. The programme was a very good one, and was as follows:—Opening chorus "Down the River," by the Company; song" The Old Home and what it used to be," Mr. J. Thorpe; comic song "0 my darling Clexentine," Mr. H. W. Tate; song "Poor Old Joe, ' Mr. R. C. Rosenberg; comic song "The Nigger's Wedding," Mr. H. Bann: song "White Wings," Mr. J. Jeffs; comic song "The Penny Showman," Mr. 11. W. Tate; song " Haste ! darling haste !" Mr. R. 11. Williams; comic song "I'll never go home any more," Mr. H. Bann; song "Only once more," Mr. R. H. Williams; comic song "The Calabar," Mr. 11. W. Tate; stump speech "The Temperance Question," Mr. W. Beckett; Comic song "Don't you take liberties," Mr. H. Bann. A laughable sketch was given at the close entitled 66 Waxination gratis "which highly amused those present. The best songs (encores) were sung by Messrs. H. Bann (" The niggers wedding,") J. Jeffs (" White wings,") H. W. Tate (" The penny showman;') encored, and R. H. Williams (" Haste darling haste," and Only once more.") A stump speech by Mr. W. Beckett was very amusing, the local hits being keenly appreciated. The jokes and conundrums of the corner men Messrs. Bann and Tate were very good, and Mr. Williams whom we understand has had sole management of the whole affair is deserving of great praise. Mr. R. Clarke was interlocater, and Mr. W. Grounds presided at the harmonium.

div.head: FRODSTIAM.
div.p: FRODSTIAM.

FRHEMASONRY.-At a meeting of the Cholmondeley Lodge (No 1908), held in Frodsham, on Monday even- ing, Mr. Hugh F. Gooch, mechanical engineer, was initiated in the first degree of Freemasonry; Mr. C. C. Henshaw, civil engineer, was passed to the second degree, and Mr. Samuel Davies was raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason.

ACCIDENI" TO A FOOTBALL PIA/AR AT FRODSHAISL—On Saturday afternoon, whilst a football match between the Frodsham Assoctation and Grosvenor House Clubs was being played on the Frodsham ground, Mr. R. D. Mad- dock, solicitor, of Runcorn and Chester, received a severe injury by a fall, which resulted in one of his legs being broken just above the ankle.

LATEST NEWS.
Father Kennedy was re-arrested on Friday at Meelin, and taken to Mallow. Sir William Pearse has passed a good day, and has taken nourishmeat well. _

A Cabinet Council' was held on Friday, when the Ministers had under consideration the question of increasing the British force at Suakim. Lord Tollemache attained his eighty-third birthday on Friday. His lordship, who is staying at Peckforton Castle, Cheshire, is in excellent health, and received numerous birthdaycongratulations. Three men were arrested on Friday for the Rathfriland murder, which is attributed to aland dispute. A witness named Morgan who was arrested, and subsequently released gave evidence yesterday, and the case was re- manded. Euscriosz iNTRLLIGENCE.—Friday next, the 14th inst., is fixed for the polling at Maidstone. The candidates are Mr. Barker (G L) and Mr. Cornwallis (C). The funeral of Major Ross, the late member, took place on Friday at Kensal Green Cemetery, London. The first meeting of the New Council of the National Union of Conservative Associations for 1888-89 was held yesterday at London, under the presidency of the Duke of Norfolk. Sir Albert Rollett was elected chairman for the ensuing year. Messrs. J. Dixon Hartland, Byrom Reed, and Stuard Wortley were elected vice-chairmen. THR MILDNESS OF THE SRASON.—In the garden of the Hermitage, Neston, Cheshire, may now be seen a straw- berry bed ia full bloom, with fruit formed as large as gooseberries; in another garden not far from the Hermit, age, ;green peas are growing and furnishing good dishes. •

Two MEN SCALDED TO DEATH.—Whilst a swimming competition was taking place on Thursday night at Warrender Private Baths, Edinburgh, the noise of escaping steam was heard in the boiler house, and an investigation showed that two men had met with a terrible accident. To repair the boiler they had incau- tiously opened a manhole, and a sudden rush of steam scalded them fatally. They died in great agony, one or: Thursday nighttand the other on Friday morning. Tits SHEEHY INCIDENT.—The "Freeman's Journal" publishes the text of the report of the Committee on the Sheehy incident, which expresses the opinioa that Con- stable Sullivan's action was a breach of privilege, but under all the circumstances they do not recommend any action by the House against Sullivan. The Privilege Committee yesterday agreed, by a majority of one, to report that the Executive didn't take the precaution of issuing proper instructions to the Irish police for the observance of due respect to the House of Commons. TRH PARNELL Comussiox.—The Parnell Commission re-assembled on Friday. when Patrick Molloy, who was brou.ht up under arrest, was examined. He said he had never been a Fenian. and that, he had never been intro- duced into a society by James Carey. He neither knew Carey, Ford, nor Frank Byrne, but the latter obtained hiss a situation in America in 1883.—John Walker, assistant to Mr. Beauchamp, solicitor, was called, but the president, after Molloy's statement, said the evidence as to Molloy's previous statements were valueless. Evidence of the shooting of Mr. Feerick. near Holly. mount was then given. The remainder of the day was devoted to the recital of outrages of the usual character, various farmers deposing to visits of armed men, &c., in the course of which they were shot at, or otherwise maltreated.

, M. BRIGHT'S ILLmiss.—Mr. Bright had a tolerably good night on Thursday, coughing less. His general con dition is unchanged. Mr. Bright's personal reconcilia- tion with Mr. Gladstone was, the "Pall Mall Gazette" understands, of a very touching character. He sent specially for a member of his family, who was charged to deliver his message to Mr. Gladstone. The tears started to the sick man's eyes as he gave his message to his friend of so many years and his leader in so many fights. It is pleasant to know that, in spite of the tedious and anxious character of his illness, Mr. Bright suffers very little pain, and is in full possession of all his faculties. Only two or three days ago he had twelve columns of the Parnell Commission report read to him, and this exercise had no depressing effect on the invalid whatever. One may thirely hope after this that there is plenty of life in the old Tribune yet.—The Press Associ- ation Rochdale correspondent adds that of late Mr. Bright has been greatly troubled by insomnia, the mild weather prevailing being oppressive to him, as he is feverish. At three yesterday afternoon, 'a coriespon- dent had an interview with Dr. Hayle, and was informed that Mr. Bright was stronger than he was two days ago, but that his condition was still critical. It remained about the same as at 10 a.m.

div.head: HAVANT MURDER.
div.p: THE HAVANT MURDER.

The inquest on the body of the boy Searle was resumed at Havant yesterday.—Captain Boyd deposed that he passed the spot where the body was found on the night of the murder, at about ten minutes past six. If the body had been there then he must have seen it, or fallen over it. He met a man about, five feet nine, who had the appearance of a navvy, coming from the direction of the Town Hall. Witness heard no cries, and met neither Searle or Husband. The child Farman, whose evidence was refused at the magisterial examina- tion, also gave evidence. The inquest was adjourned until Wednesday.

div.head: DUEL IN FRANCE.
div.p: A DUEL IN FRANCE.

Pam, FRIDAY.—In consequence of an altercation during yesterday's sitting of the Paris Municipal Council, a duel was fought with swords this morning between two of its members—M. Menorval, Boulangist, and M. Chautemps, Irreconcilable. The ratter was slightly wounded in the arm. THE SIEGE OF SUAKIM.

div.head: AN ARTIST OF 71,31
div.p: AN ARTIST OF 71,31
GRAPHIC
KILLED.

A Suakim correspondent says that Mr. Wade, an English artist, who sent illustrations to the " Graphic," was struck by a bullet from the enemy's trenches, while near Shatta date, on Thursday afternoon. The wound proved fflortal, Mr. Wade expiring from its effects at three o'clock on Friday morning. A bugler has been killed, while exercising, by a shell from the enemy.
YESTERDArS PARLIAMENT. HOUSE' OF COMMONS.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. Qtritsrmws.—Mr.. JACKSON, replying to Mr. Howard Vincent, declined to adopt a suggestion to impose a license on the employment of foreigners as servants in England.—Mr. RITCHIE. replying to Sir W. Foster, said that it was not. in his power to grant returns of represent- ations maae to Sinitary Authorities, under the Allot- ment Act, asking them to take proceedings under the Act.—Sir M. H. BEACH. replying to Mr. S. G. Campbell, said that he did not think the Government would with- draw the clauses in the Employers' Liability Act extend- ing the Act to seamen.---Afr. A. BALFOUR, replying to Mr. Sexton, said that the Irish Attorney General would not send up a bill to the grand jury against the policeman Swindell, against whom a verdict a wilful murder had beeirreturned by a coroner's jury, until after the fullest inquiry had been made.—Mr. W. H. Slim replying to a question, said that it had been decided not to make any alteration in the Bank Holiday Act by changing the holiday this year from Wednesday the 26th, to Monday the 24th of December.—The Home Secretary replying to Sir G. Cambell, declined to make public the proceedings be had instituted regarding the Edlingham Burglary Case.—Mr. A. BALFOUR, replying to a question, said that if application was made to Judge Boyd to release Maroney on the ground of danger to his health, he would hear it, and order his discharge if necessary. THE PROGRESS OF BUSINESS.—Mr. W. H. SMITH sail that the Scotch Estimates would be taken next Tuesday and Wednesday. The discussion of the Sunday Closing Act would be taken at an evening sitting on Friday, the 14th. He could say nothing further beyond a promise already given as regarded the Scotch Universities Bill. He had received a memorial signed by 22 Scotch mem- bers not to proceed with the Bill*, and 21 were for going on with it. NEW Warr.—A New Writ was issued for Maidstone. EMPLOYERS LIABILITY BILL.—OR this Bill being considered as amended, Mr. BROAD/117E9T strenuously opposed the Bill proceeding, and moved that the report should be considered that day three months.' He censured Governmeti for not accepting the proposals that had been submitted to them as regarded clause three, which, if they had, would have removed all difficulty, and enabled the Bill to Oct through the present stage within a few hours. rr the Bill passed in face of the opposition of the great majority of people concerned, they would immediately denounce it, and the House through which it became law, and would re-commence an agitation for a measure that would do justice .and equity to all persons. He denounced the third clause as an attempt to impose on thepeople of this country the German system of com- pulsory insurance, which would sap the independence of. , English workmen. He believed that one of the objects lof the Bill was to strike at the root of the Trades I Unionism, and if it was passed the working-classes et the country would do all ia their power to render it in- , operative. As regards seamen the Bill was so over I safe-guarded as practically to leave that class entirely unprotected.—Mr. JOICEY, as a large employer of labour, seconded Mr. Baciannostsv's motion.—Mr. BRAM/MOH accepted responsibility for all the recommendations that the Government had adopted. He denied that :Mr. Broadhurst represented the true feeling of the workmen regarding the bill. The HOME SECRETARY defended the bill. Discussion on the bill was continued till a late hour.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. TO THE ELECTORS OF TIIE DARESBURY DIVISION. LADIES AND GICNTLESIEN,—I have been requested to come forward as a candidate for your division in the new County Council, and I feel that on public grounds it is my duty to comply with such request. I have been connected with your division for nearly half a century, and I am fully conversant with the rights and interests of the ratepayers in relation to County matters. I consider that all rates levied for County purposes should be under the control of a body responsible to the ratepayers, and should be administered economically in the interests of such ratepayers. The Act constituting the Council, takes out of the hands of the Justices of the Peace all matters relating to County gov- ernment, with the exception of criminal administration, appeals, &c., and a joint control of the police by a committee formed of certain Justices and certain members of the County Council ; all other County business will be in the hands of the new Council. The public positions which I hold, and my general know- ledge of public business, justify me in saying that I should be able to render valuable services to the ratepayers of the county, and it is upon this ground, and not from any personal ambi- tion, that I am desirous for a seat upon the Council. There are certain matters affecting the interest and con- venience of occupiers of land and owners of stock which require amendment, so as to avoid the inconvenience at present existing as to the transfer of stock from one part of the county to another, and the regulations under the C, utxtTious Diseases (Animals) Act, require, I think,very careful ray don. If I am returned for your division I shall am alt times publicly ventilate all matters which may prejudicial im affect the constituency of the Dares bury Division. I am, Ladies and Gentleme Yours faithfully, 11. LI NARER. Prodsham, 6th December. 1888.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE DIVISION OF RUNCORN SOUTH. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN.—Having received a requisition signed by a numerous and influential body of Electors, asking me to come forward as a Candidate for the representa- tion of your Division, I have much pleasure in accedingto their wishes. My life-long connection with, and residence in Runcorn, have afforded me abundant opportunities of learning the requirements of the town and district generally. As a Justice of Ate Peace, I have been appointed a mem- ber of, and am now serving upon, sevexal of the most Important of the county committees, and this has enabled me to make myself conversant with the administration of county business. Allow me to correct an Impression which I understand has gained currency in the town, that I am coming forward as a Conservative. I am much opposed to politics being introduced into what I consider a purely local matter, and I should be glad to see the elections conducted without any display of party feeling. Should you do me the honour to return me as your representstive, you may rely upon my best exertions to promote economy and efficiency in carrying out the provisions of this most important Act. I have the honour to be, Yours faithfully, JOHN DRUNDRIT, The Highlands, Runcorn, November 29th, 1888.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE DARESBURY ELECTORAL DIVISION. LIDIFS AND GENTLEMEN,—A requisition, numerously signed by farmers and other electors, has bean presented, nviting me to allow myself to be nominated to the office of Councillor for the Daresbury Electoral Division in January next, to which I accede. Having acted as a magistrate for nearly 23 years, having served on the County Police and Licensing Committees for some years, and haring been chairman of the Daresbury Highway Board for 20 years, lam able to say, with perfect good faith, that I have had some experience in county and district business. Should you do me the honour of electing me, I will under- take faithfully, and to the best of my ability, to discharge the very important duties that will devolve upon me as a mem- ber of the County Council, especially in all matters affecting the important agricultural interest of this district, and at the same time It will be my aim to promote efficiency, with striet regard to proper economy, in all matters concerning till district and county interests generally. I have the honour to remain Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, IiIDWARD OREENALL, Grappenhall Hall, November 24th, 1828.
